title: Course Syllabus
text:
Reading Load
Each class meeting has two assigned readings:

A chapter from Oatley (the course textbook) — roughly 25–30 pages, providing the conceptual and theoretical foundation for the day.
A scholarly article — typically a peer-reviewed journal article or book chapter that applies, complicates, or extends the chapter’s argument with contemporary evidence or a current policy case.

Plan for roughly 40–55 pages of reading per class day. You should complete both readings before the class session in which they are discussed. Wednesdays are non-meeting reading days that provide time to catch up if you fall behind.
Each student will sign up on Day 1 to present and lead discussion on one of the scholarly articles (see Article Presentation below). Note that Day 1 (July 6) has no second reading — that session is reserved for course logistics and a discussion of how to read political-economy scholarship. I will model the article presentation on Day 2 so you have a clear example before signing up for your own slot.

title: Course Syllabus
text:
Class Sessions (2 hours, 10 minutes)
Each session typically includes:

Lecture and concept review on the day’s chapter (about 75 minutes)
A student-led article presentation and discussion (about 20 minutes; not every day)
Either an in-class writing activity and debrief (Mondays, Tuesdays, and Thursdays) or a quiz (Fridays of weeks 1, 2, and 3) — about 30 minutes

Together these run about 125 minutes, inside our 130-minute block. Active participation is essential in this format. Come prepared to discuss the assigned readings and engage with case examples.

title: Course Syllabus
text:
Assignment Details

Quizzes (30% — 10% each)
Three quizzes given at the end of class on the Fridays of weeks 1, 2, and 3 — July 10, July 17, and July 24. Each quiz covers material from that week (chapters and articles). Quizzes consist of multiple-choice and short-answer questions and serve as comprehension checks that build toward the final exam.


Final Exam (25%)
Date: Friday, July 31, in class. The final is cumulative. It includes multiple-choice questions, short-answer questions on concept application, and an applied question grounded in a contemporary policy scenario.


Participation & Engagement (20% — 5% per week)
Active engagement is essential in an intensive online format. Participation is evaluated weekly and includes:

Attending class sessions prepared to discuss the assigned readings
Contributing thoughtful comments and questions during lecture and discussion
Engaging substantively with peers’ article presentations
Participating in small-group exercises and chat-based activities

Given the compressed format, missing even one class represents significant lost participation.


In-Class Writing Activities (15%)
Each Monday, Tuesday, and Thursday includes a short (~10-minute) in-class writing activity tied to the day’s material. Timing varies — sometimes the activity opens class to focus the reading, sometimes it comes toward the end of class as a synthesis check on a core concept from that day’s lecture. Prompts may ask you to summarize a key argument, apply a concept to a contemporary case, or stake out a position on a debate from the chapter.
Activities are graded credit / no-credit on a √, √+, √– scale:

√+ — Engages substantively with the material and presents a clear, supported response
√ — Completes the activity with evidence of having done the reading
√– — Submitted but missing key elements or showing limited engagement

Activities are not accepted late and cannot be made up except in cases of documented absence cleared in advance.


Article Presentation & Discussion (10%)
Most class days include one scholarly article (Reading 2) on a contemporary issue. Day 1 (July 6) is the exception — that session is reserved for course logistics and orientation. Each student will sign up on Day 1 to present one article and lead a 15–20 minute discussion of it. I will model the first presentation on Day 2 (July 7) so you have a clear example before your slot comes up.
Your presentation should:

Briefly summarize the article’s argument, evidence, and conclusion (5 minutes)
Connect the article to the day’s textbook chapter and broader course themes
Pose 2–3 discussion questions to the class
Facilitate the resulting discussion

Evaluation considers preparation, clarity, depth of engagement with the reading, and quality of discussion facilitation.

Attendance
Given the compressed format, missing one class session represents a full week of a regular semester course. More than one unexcused absence will negatively impact your grade. If you must miss class due to illness or emergency, contact me as soon as possible.

Late Work
In-class writing prompts cannot be made up. Quizzes and the final exam can only be rescheduled with advance notice and a documented, legitimate reason.

Academic Integrity
All work must be your own. Plagiarism or cheating will result in failure of the assignment and possible course failure. Consult IU’s academic integrity policies if you have questions about proper citation or collaboration.

Generative AI Policy
Generative AI tools may not be used during in-class writing prompts, quizzes, or the final exam. You may use AI tools to help you understand assigned readings outside of class — but you are responsible for verifying everything an AI tells you against the actual readings, and you remain responsible for your own learning.

title: Achievements and Challenges of Global Capitalism
text:
Today’s Plan — Our Last Session



Today’s Big Question


Global capitalism has delivered historic gains — can the system that produced them survive the backlash against them?








Section
What we'll cover




1 · The Achievements
Poverty's historic fall, emerging Asia, and global convergence


2 · The Distributional Challenge
Globalization's losers, the China shock, inequality within rich states


3 · The Sustainability Challenge
Growth against climate limits, and the global public-goods problem


4 · The Political Backlash
Populism, economic nationalism, and the fraying liberal order


5 · Is the Liberal Order Sustainable?
Oatley's scenarios: reform, fragmentation, or managed globalization


6 · Course Capstone: The Central Analytic Frame
Society-centered vs. state-centered, across the whole course


7 · Closing & the Final Exam
What we built, and how the cumulative final is structured








Welcome to our last class. Today is unusual, and I want to flag the format up front, because this session does double duty. On one level it is a normal chapter day: we are reading Oatley’s Chapter 16, “Achievements and Challenges of Global Capitalism,” which is his concluding chapter and is built to be exactly the kind of stock-taking we want at the end of a course. But on another level this is the capstone — the day where we step back from the individual units on trade, money, multinationals, and finance and ask what the whole picture adds up to. So I have structured the day to move from the achievements of the modern global economy, through the three great challenges to it, to the political backlash those challenges have produced, and finally to a synthesis of the analytical toolkit you have spent four weeks building.
Hold the Big Question the whole way through, because it is genuinely open and it is the question the chapter is wrestling with. Global capitalism — the open, integrated world economy built since 1945 and turbocharged after the Cold War — has produced gains that, measured against all of human history, are simply extraordinary. We are going to be honest and specific about those gains, because the backlash makes it easy to forget them. But the same system has produced losers, strained the planet, and generated a political reaction that is now visibly fraying the liberal order that made it possible. The question is whether the system can reform itself enough to survive that reaction, or whether we are watching the early stages of its unwinding.
Logistics for the day: you have a writing prompt at the start of class, as usual on a Thursday. There is no quiz — the last quiz was Friday. The next and final assessment is the cumulative final exam, which is tomorrow, Friday, at our normal online meeting time, and I will spend the last few minutes today walking you through its structure and how to prepare. Let us begin where the honest story has to begin: with the achievements.

title: Achievements and Challenges of Global Capitalism
section: Before We Start: A Ten-Minute Write
text:
Before We Start: A Ten-Minute Write



Writing prompt. Global capitalism has lifted more people out of poverty than any system in history — and it is also more politically unpopular in rich democracies than at any point since the 1930s.
Before today’s lecture makes the case for both sides in detail: which force do you think wins over the next twenty years — continued, if uneven, integration, or a genuine retreat into economic nationalism? Give one piece of evidence for your prediction, drawn from anywhere in the course.






Write for about ten minutes from intuition — you don’t need today’s evidence yet. We’ll come back to what you wrote when we reach Section 5.




Run this cold, before any lecturing — the point is to get a documented prediction on record before the chapter’s evidence arrives, not to test what students already know. Take a rough show of hands after the ten minutes: who predicted continued integration, who predicted fragmentation, who predicted something messier in between. Don’t resolve it now. The payoff comes in Section 5, when Oatley’s three scenarios — reform, fragmentation, managed globalization — give students the vocabulary to revisit what they wrote and see whether the lecture’s evidence pushed them toward or away from their own prediction. That’s the point of asking this before rather than after: the surprise of being confirmed or corrected is what makes the capstone stick.

title: Achievements and Challenges of Global Capitalism
section: The Headline Achievement: Poverty’s Historic Fall
text:
The Headline Achievement: Poverty’s Historic Fall










Figure 1









The single biggest fact of our era. The share of humanity in extreme poverty fell from roughly 40% around 1980 to under 10% by the late 2010s — well over a billion people.






This is not the whole story, and we will complicate it. But any honest account of global capitalism has to start here.





I want to open the achievements section with the fact that, in my view, every educated person should know and that is too easily lost in our current mood of pessimism. Over the four decades from roughly 1980 to 2019, the share of the world’s population living in extreme poverty — by the World Bank’s definition, surviving on less than a couple of dollars a day at constant prices — fell from something like forty percent to under ten percent. In absolute terms, even as world population grew by billions, the number of people in extreme poverty dropped by well over a billion. There is no precedent for a material improvement of that scale and speed in human history. I have drawn this chart as illustrative — the exact figures depend on the poverty line and the year, and the Bank has revised its lines over time — but the shape is not in dispute. This happened, and it happened during the era of deepening global economic integration.
I am deliberately starting here, and starting emphatically, for two reasons. First, because it is true, and intellectual honesty requires us to put the central achievement on the table before we start dissecting the failures. The backlash literature, and frankly the mood of the moment, makes it easy to talk as though globalization has been an unbroken story of loss. It has not. Second, because the rest of today’s argument is sharper if you hold this gain clearly. The challenges we are about to discuss — distribution, sustainability, political backlash — are not arguments that global capitalism failed. They are arguments about who captured the gains, what the gains cost, and whether the political coalition that sustained the system can hold. You cannot evaluate those arguments fairly if you have forgotten the magnitude of what the system delivered. So: start here.

title: Achievements and Challenges of Global Capitalism
section: Where the Gains Came From: Emerging Asia and Convergence
text:
Where the Gains Came From: Emerging Asia and Convergence


Two structural shifts drove the gains:

The rise of emerging Asia — China above all, then India and Southeast Asia — pulled hundreds of millions into the global middle class
Growth through integration — these economies grew by joining world trade and investment flows, not by withdrawing from them
Cross-country convergence — for the first time, large poor countries grew faster than rich ones, narrowing the gap between nations





The mechanism is our whole course. Trade access (Chs. 2–7), inward FDI (Chs. 8–9), a functioning monetary order (Chs. 10–13), and capital inflows (Chs. 14–15) were the channels of catch-up.






Falling between-country inequality is the flip side of the poverty story. The world’s poor were concentrated in the countries that grew fastest.





Where did that historic poverty decline come from? It was not evenly spread across the planet — it was overwhelmingly driven by the rise of emerging Asia, and within that, above all by China, followed by India and the economies of Southeast Asia. China alone accounts for the majority of the global poverty reduction of the last forty years. And the mechanism matters enormously for a course on international political economy, because these economies did not grow by turning inward and cutting themselves off from the world. They grew by joining it — by integrating into global trade, by hosting waves of foreign direct investment, by exporting manufactured goods into open Western markets, and by operating within a functioning international monetary and financial system. The channels of their catch-up are literally the chapters of this course. That is not a coincidence I am imposing on the material; it is the substantive point.
This connects to a finding that surprises students. If you ask whether global inequality has risen or fallen over this period, the answer depends on which inequality you mean. Inequality between countries — the gap in average incomes between rich nations and poor nations — has actually narrowed over the last few decades, precisely because the large poor countries, where most of the world’s poor people lived, grew faster than the rich ones. That is convergence, and it is genuinely good news. Remember that point, because in the very next section we are going to look at a different inequality measure — inequality within advanced economies — that moved in the opposite direction. The headline of the achievements section is that the system delivered convergence between nations and a historic fall in poverty. The headline of the challenges section is that it did so while widening divides inside the rich democracies that built it. Both are true at once, and the tension between them is the politics of our moment.

title: Achievements and Challenges of Global Capitalism
section: The Politics of Domestic Winners and Losers
text:
The Politics of Domestic Winners and Losers


We have known since Chapter 4 that trade has distributional effects:

Trade raises aggregate welfare but redistributes — some groups gain, others lose
The losses are concentrated (a closed factory, a hollowed-out town); the gains are diffuse (slightly cheaper goods for everyone)
The theory never promised that everyone wins — only that winners could compensate losers
In practice, compensation rarely happened





This is not a surprise — it is Chapter 4. The society-centered approach told us exactly who would resist trade and why. The distributional challenge is that prediction coming true.






The political problem: concentrated losers organize; diffuse winners do not. That asymmetry drives the backlash in Section 4.











Figure 2







Now we turn to the first great challenge, and I want to frame it in a way that pulls the course together rather than treating it as a fresh topic, because it is not fresh — we have known this since the second week. Go back to Chapter 4, the society-centered approach to trade. The whole point of that chapter was that trade liberalization is not a free lunch in distributional terms. Trade raises aggregate national welfare — the pie gets bigger — but it does so by reorganizing the economy, which means it produces winners and losers within a country. Whether you used the Stolper-Samuelson factor model or the Ricardo-Viner sector model, the prediction was the same: some groups gain from openness and some lose, and they will line up politically on opposite sides accordingly. The theory of gains from trade never claimed that every individual is better off. It claimed only that the winners gain more than the losers lose, so that in principle the winners could compensate the losers and everyone could come out ahead.
The phrase to underline is “in principle.” In practice, across most advanced economies, that compensation largely did not happen. The aggregate gains from trade were real, but they flowed disproportionately to capital, to skilled workers, to consumers as a diffuse benefit, and to the owners of globally competitive firms — while the losses landed hard and concentrated on particular workers, particular industries, particular regions. And here is the political asymmetry that Chapter 4 set up and that drives the rest of today: the losers from trade are concentrated and visible — a closed plant, a town that loses its anchor employer — which makes them easy to organize and to mobilize politically. The winners are diffuse — all of us paying a little less for goods — which makes them politically inert. Concentrated interests beat diffuse ones in politics. So the distributional challenge is not a failure of the theory. It is the theory’s central prediction coming true, and then colliding with a political system that did little to cushion the people on the losing side.
The chart in the right column is the “elephant graph” from Lakner and Milanovic’s work on global income distribution, 1988 to 2008. It puts a number on exactly the tension this slide describes. Read it by global income percentile, not by country: the strongest growth is in the middle of the global distribution, which is overwhelmingly the newly emerging middle classes of China, India, and the rest of Asia. Growth then dips sharply around the 75th to 90th percentiles of the global distribution — and that band is where the lower-middle and working classes of rich countries like the United States sit globally, even though they are not poor by domestic standards. Growth picks back up again only at the very top, the global 1%. So the same twenty years that produced the historic poverty decline from Section 1 also produced near-stagnant growth for a specific slice of people in rich countries — precisely the people whose politics we are about to discuss. Hold onto this chart, because it is the empirical version of the “concentrated losses, diffuse gains” story on the left.

title: Achievements and Challenges of Global Capitalism
section: The China Shock: When the Prediction Got Sharp
text:
The China Shock: When the Prediction Got Sharp


China’s entry into world trade (WTO accession, 2001) was a shock of unusual size and speed:

Research on the U.S. “China shock” finds sharp, persistent local losses where import competition hit
Affected communities saw lower employment and wages that did not bounce back as the textbook adjustment story predicted
Workers did not smoothly relocate to new jobs and new places





Why it mattered politically. The losses were geographically concentrated, slow to heal, and clearly attributable to trade — the ideal fuel for an anti-globalization politics.






The aggregate gains from China trade were still large. The point is distribution and adjustment, not that trade was a mistake.





The sharpest empirical illustration of the distributional challenge, and the one that has reshaped how economists themselves talk about trade, is what is now called the China shock. China’s integration into the world economy, capped by its accession to the WTO in 2001, was not a normal incremental trade liberalization. It was the entry of an economy of unprecedented size, with an enormous low-wage labor force, into global manufacturing supply chains, and it happened fast. A body of research — the most cited associated with David Autor, David Dorn, and Gordon Hanson — examined what happened to American local labor markets that were most exposed to the surge of Chinese import competition. And the findings genuinely surprised the profession, because they did not match the reassuring textbook adjustment story.
The textbook story says that when imports displace workers in one industry, those workers move — to other industries, to other regions, to new opportunities created by the cheaper imports and the expanded export sectors — and after a painful but temporary transition, the economy is better off and the workers are reabsorbed. What the China-shock research found instead was that the local losses were sharp, geographically concentrated, and persistent. Communities hit hardest by import competition saw lasting declines in manufacturing employment, depressed wages, and elevated joblessness that did not bounce back over a decade or more. Workers did not smoothly relocate; many stayed put as their local economies hollowed out. Now, I want to be careful and fair, which is the right callout: this is not evidence that trade with China was a net loss for the United States. The aggregate gains — cheaper goods, more efficient production, gains to exporters and consumers — were large and real. The finding is about distribution and adjustment: the gains and losses were distributed very unevenly, and the adjustment mechanism that was supposed to spread the gains around worked far worse than the models assumed. And politically, a loss that is concentrated, persistent, and obviously attributable to foreign trade is precisely the kind of grievance that fuels an anti-globalization movement. Keep that link in mind; it pays off in Section 4.

title: Achievements and Challenges of Global Capitalism
section: The Two Inequalities, Side by Side
text:
The Two Inequalities, Side by Side






Between countries
Within rich countries




What it measures
Income gaps between countries
Income gaps inside advanced economies


Direction since ~1980
Narrowed — convergence
Widened in many rich democracies


Who it helped / hurt
Helped the global poor in fast-growing emerging economies
Hurt lower-skill workers in import-competing regions


Political consequence
Underwrites the 'globalization works' case
Fuels the backlash inside the system's own core










The paradox in one line: the same era that made the world more equal between nations made many rich nations less equal within themselves. That tension is the politics of globalization.




This table is the conceptual hinge of the distributional section, and if you remember one slide from the first half of today, make it this one, because it resolves an apparent contradiction that confuses people in public debate. You will hear one person say globalization reduced inequality and another say it increased inequality, and they are both pointing at real data — they are just measuring different things. So we have to be precise about which inequality we mean.
The left column is inequality between countries: the gap between rich nations and poor nations, measured by average incomes. That gap narrowed over the last forty years, because the big poor countries grew faster than the rich ones — the convergence and poverty story from Section 1. By this measure, the era of globalization made the world more equal, and it helped the global poor enormously. The right column is inequality within advanced economies: the gap between high earners and low earners inside a country like the United States, the United Kingdom, or many others. That gap widened in many rich democracies over the same period. Trade was not the only cause — technological change and skill-biased automation matter at least as much, and honest scholars debate the relative weights — but import competition, including the China shock, was a real contributor for the workers and regions on the losing end.
Now read the two columns together, because the paradox is the whole point and it is the bottom callout. The same integrated global economy that compressed inequality between nations stretched inequality within many of the nations that built it. And that combination is politically combustible in a specific way: the people who lost out are voters and citizens inside the wealthy democracies — the very societies whose political support the liberal order needs in order to survive. The system delivered its biggest gains to people who do not vote in American or European elections, while imposing concentrated, visible losses on people who do. You can see, just from this table, why the backlash erupted where it did. The winners of globalization between nations cannot vote to defend it inside the countries where its political fate is being decided. Keep that in view — it sets up Section 4 directly.

title: Achievements and Challenges of Global Capitalism
text:
Growth Against the Planet’s Limits


The growth that lifted billions also carries an ecological bill:

Rising output and consumption drove rising greenhouse-gas emissions and resource use
Climate change is the defining case, but not the only one — biodiversity loss, water stress, pollution
The very industrialization that powered catch-up growth is the largest single driver of the emissions problem





The hard tension. We cannot simply tell developing countries to stop growing — growth is how poverty fell. But the historical path of growth is environmentally unsustainable.






This is not anti-growth doom-mongering. It is a genuine trade-off the next generation of policy has to manage, not wish away.





The second great challenge is sustainability, and I want to present it without melodrama, because the topic invites both denial and panic and neither is useful for analysis. The basic fact is straightforward. The growth that lifted more than a billion people out of poverty was, historically, fossil-fueled industrial growth. More output meant more energy use, which meant more greenhouse-gas emissions, which is the principal driver of climate change. It also meant rising resource extraction, water stress, pollution, and pressure on biodiversity. Climate is the defining case because it is global and effectively irreversible on human timescales, but it is not the only ecological cost. The uncomfortable truth is that the very engine of the achievement we celebrated in Section 1 — rapid industrialization in emerging economies — is also the single largest contributor to the environmental challenge.
The tension this creates, in the top callout, is genuinely hard, and I want you to feel its difficulty rather than resolve it cheaply. You cannot simply tell developing countries to stop growing. Growth is how poverty fell; growth is how hundreds of millions of people got electricity, clean water, schooling, and longer lives. There is a deep equity problem in the rich countries, having burned fossil fuels for two centuries to get rich, turning to the countries now industrializing and telling them they may not do the same. At the same time, the historical, carbon-intensive path of growth is not indefinitely sustainable — the atmosphere is a finite sink. So this is not a problem you solve by picking growth or picking the planet. It is a trade-off that has to be managed: decoupling growth from emissions through technology and policy, financing a transition in the developing world, and doing it fast enough to matter. The reason I am putting this in a political-economy course, and not leaving it to the climate scientists, is the next slide — because the deepest obstacle to managing this trade-off is not technological. It is a problem of political economy that this course has equipped you to name.

title: Achievements and Challenges of Global Capitalism
section: Why Climate Is So Hard: A Global Public Good
text:
Why Climate Is So Hard: A Global Public Good


Climate stability is a global public good — and that creates a brutal collective-action problem:

Non-excludable: a stable climate benefits everyone, payer or not
Free-riding: every state would prefer that others bear the cost of cutting emissions
No world government can compel cooperation — the same anarchy problem from the trade and monetary chapters
Costs are paid now and locally; benefits are diffuse, global, and in the future





You already have this framework. This is the same cooperation-under-anarchy problem as the WTO (Ch. 3) and monetary cooperation (Ch. 11) — now with the highest possible stakes.






That is why climate agreements are voluntary and underpowered: there is no enforcer, only the same fragile cooperation we studied all term.





Here is where the sustainability challenge becomes a political-economy problem rather than an engineering one, and where your toolkit from this course does real work. A stable climate is a global public good. Recall the definition of a public good: it is non-excludable, meaning you cannot stop anyone from enjoying it once it exists, and non-rival, meaning one person’s enjoyment does not diminish another’s. A stable climate is the textbook example — it benefits every country on earth whether or not that country paid anything to produce it. And public goods, as you know, are chronically undersupplied, because of free-riding. Every individual state faces the same temptation: the benefits of a stable climate flow to me regardless of whether I cut my own emissions, while the costs of cutting — to my industries, my consumers, my growth — are mine alone to bear. So each state’s narrowly rational move is to let everyone else do the cutting. If every state reasons that way, nobody cuts enough, and the public good is undersupplied. That is the collective-action problem at the heart of climate.
And now notice that this is exactly the same analytical structure we have used all term, in the top callout. Cooperation under anarchy. The world has no government that can compel states to cooperate; international cooperation has to be self-enforcing, sustained by reciprocity and institutions rather than by a global police force. We saw this with the WTO in Chapter 3 — how do you sustain open trade when each state is tempted to cheat with protection? We saw it with monetary cooperation in Chapter 11 — how do you coordinate exchange-rate and macro policy when each state has incentives to defect? Climate is the same problem with two features that make it the hardest version: the stakes are existential, and the structure of costs and benefits is maximally unfavorable. The costs of action are paid now, locally, by identifiable groups who will resist; the benefits are diffuse, global, and arrive in a future beyond most electoral horizons. That is why our climate agreements — Kyoto, Paris — are voluntary pledges with weak enforcement rather than binding commitments with teeth. There is no enforcer. There is only the same fragile, reciprocity-based cooperation we have studied all course, now asked to carry the heaviest load it has ever faced. You did not need a new framework to understand the politics of climate. You needed the one you already have.

title: Achievements and Challenges of Global Capitalism
section: The Backlash Against the Open Economy
text:
The Backlash Against the Open Economy


Since the 2010s, a broad reaction against economic openness:

Populism — channeling the grievances of globalization’s losers against elites and outsiders
Economic nationalism — tariffs, “buy national,” reshoring, industrial policy
The return of protectionism — the U.S.–China trade war, broad tariff regimes, supply-chain “de-risking”
A fraying of the rules-based liberal order: a stalled WTO, weakened dispute settlement (Ch. 3)





The throughline of the course. The backlash is the political demand generated by the distributional losses of Section 2, expressed through the institutions of Chapters 2–5.






The order was always political, not natural. It was built by states and sustained by a coalition — and coalitions can come apart.



🎧 Today’s podcast — Trade Talks ep. 27, Dani Rodrik on “What Are Trade Deals For?” — the trilemma behind the backlash, from the economist who saw it coming.


The fourth section is the political backlash, and the reason it comes right after distribution and sustainability is that it is, in large part, the political consequence of them. Since roughly the mid-2010s — symbolically marked by the Brexit referendum and the 2016 U.S. election, but much broader than any two events — we have seen a sustained reaction against the open global economy across many advanced democracies. It has several faces. There is populism, which I would define here as a politics that pits a virtuous “people” against a corrupt “elite” and frequently against foreign outsiders, and which has been very effective at channeling the grievances of globalization’s losers. There is economic nationalism, the impulse to privilege the national economy through tariffs, buy-national procurement, reshoring of supply chains, and active industrial policy — much of which we studied in Chapter 5 on the state-centered approach to trade. There is the straightforward return of protectionism, most visibly in the U.S.-China trade war and the broad tariff regimes that followed, and in the language of “de-risking” supply chains away from rivals. And there is the institutional fraying we tracked back in Chapter 3 — the stalled WTO negotiating function and the deliberate disabling of its dispute-settlement system, which you read about in the Bown and Keynes piece on why the Appellate Body was allowed to die.
Now connect it to the throughline, in the top callout, because this is the synthetic point and not just a list of headlines. The backlash is not a mysterious eruption of irrationality. It is, in substantial part, the political demand generated by the distributional losses of Section 2, finding expression through exactly the institutions and cleavages we studied in the trade chapters. The concentrated losers of globalization — Chapter 4 told us they would be concentrated and politically potent — organized and voted, and politicians responded by supplying the protection and nationalism they demanded. And here is the deeper point, in the bottom callout, and I want it to reframe the whole course for you. The liberal economic order was never a law of nature. It was a political construction — built deliberately by powerful states after 1945, embedded in institutions, and sustained by a domestic political coalition in those states that benefited from openness. Anything built by a coalition can be unbuilt when the coalition fractures. That is what we are watching. The backlash is the order’s own losers withdrawing their political consent. And that sets up the question the chapter ultimately asks. One more pointer before we move on: today’s podcast is Dani Rodrik on Trade Talks asking what trade deals are actually for — whose interests they serve and how much domestic policy space they should leave — which is the same tension between deep integration and democratic self-government that runs under everything on this slide. We’ll hear it again in the student presentation on Walter’s backlash review in a moment.

title: Achievements and Challenges of Global Capitalism
text:
Student Presentation



Over to today’s presenter


Walter (2021) — “The Backlash Against Globalization” · Annual Review of Political Science 24



Presenter: ______________________ · Q&A and class discussion to follow



The definitive review of the backlash literature — and its central claim cuts against the popular story: mass opinion has not swung sharply against globalization. The backlash is a politicization: entrepreneurs mobilizing economic losers and cultural grievance into backlash politics, with real consequences — deglobalization pressure, contested institutions, and harder international cooperation.




And now the final student presentation of the course, on Stefanie Walter’s review of the globalization backlash — the scholarly companion to the section we just finished. Let me frame it. Walter organizes everything we know about the backlash around three questions: what it is, what causes it, and what it does. On the what: she defines the backlash as the political expression of opposition to globalization — Brexit, trade-war politics, anti-globalization populism — and makes the striking point that it is not driven by a large swing in public opinion against openness; aggregate support for trade has stayed surprisingly stable. What changed is politicization: political entrepreneurs made globalization electorally salient. On the causes: she maps the debate we’ve been living in all course — economic explanations, from import competition and the China shock to the regional decline story, versus cultural explanations centered on status threat and identity — and argues they are entangled rather than rival, because economic decline feeds cultural grievance. And on the consequences: backlash politics produces governments that contest international institutions, pressure toward deglobalization, and a harder environment for the cooperation problems — trade, money, climate — we’ve studied for four weeks. Listen for how the presenter relates Walter’s politicization argument to our society-centered lens — preferences, institutions, and who mobilizes whom — and whether the evidence she reviews supports the economic or the cultural reading more strongly. This is the last presentation slot, so let’s send it off well. Q&A and discussion after.

title: Achievements and Challenges of Global Capitalism
section: Connecting Back: Coercion and the State-Centered Turn
text:
Connecting Back: Coercion and the State-Centered Turn


The backlash is also a turn toward the state-centered logic we have built all term:

States increasingly see interdependence not as mutual gain but as vulnerability and leverage
Yesterday’s class: the weaponization of interdependence — sanctions, chokepoints, export controls
Security and geopolitics now reshape trade, investment screening (Ch. 9), and even monetary policy (Ch. 13)





From efficiency to security. The defining shift of the moment: states subordinating the gains from openness to concerns about national power and security.






This is the state-centered half of the course (Chs. 5, 9, 13) reasserting itself over the society-centered logic of mutual gain.





I want to spend one slide explicitly bridging the backlash to what we did yesterday and to the state-centered thread that has run through the whole course, because Oatley’s Chapter 16 was written before the most recent turn and you should see how current events extend his argument. The backlash is not only a domestic-distributional story; it is also a geopolitical one, and it represents a shift in how states fundamentally conceive of economic interdependence. For most of the post-Cold War period, the dominant frame was the liberal, society-centered one: interdependence is mutually beneficial, trade and investment are positive-sum, and deeper integration makes everyone richer and arguably more peaceful. What we are watching now is the reassertion of a state-centered frame in which the same interdependence looks like vulnerability and like leverage. If your supply chains run through a rival, that is not just efficient — it is a chokepoint the rival can squeeze. If your adversary depends on your financial system, that dependence is a weapon you can use.
That is precisely the material from yesterday’s class on the weaponization of interdependence — Farrell and Newman, and the Drezner review on sanctions. States are increasingly willing to sacrifice the efficiency gains from openness in order to reduce strategic vulnerabilities and to acquire coercive leverage over rivals. And notice how this reaches back across the course, in the callouts. It connects to Chapter 9 and my own work on investment screening, where security concerns now lead states to block foreign acquisitions they would once have welcomed. It connects to Chapter 13 and the weaponized dollar, where monetary dominance becomes an instrument of statecraft. It connects to Chapter 5’s industrial policy, now justified in the language of national security rather than infant industries. The unifying shift, worth remembering above the details, is the subordination of the gains from openness to concerns about national power and security. The state-centered half of this course, which sometimes felt like the minority view against the liberal mainstream, is the half that is currently winning the argument in the world’s capitals. Whether that is wise is a separate question; that it is happening is not in doubt.

title: Achievements and Challenges of Global Capitalism
text:
Three Scenarios for the Future





Scenario
What it looks like
The open question




Reform & renewal
The open order survives by sharing gains better at home — real compensation for losers, stronger safety nets, retraining
Can domestic politics deliver the compensation it never delivered before?


Managed globalization
A slower, more guarded openness: selective integration, friend-shoring, security carve-outs, but trade and investment continue
Can states limit security carve-outs before they swallow openness whole?


Fragmentation
Bloc formation and decoupling — a world economy splitting along geopolitical lines, with rising costs and lost gains
Can great-power rivalry be contained before efficiency is sacrificed to security?










Oatley’s framing. The open economy is not guaranteed. Whether it survives depends on political choices — above all, whether the gains can be shared widely enough to keep the supporting coalition intact.




So: is the liberal order sustainable? Oatley does not give you a prophecy, and neither will I, because honest social science here is about laying out scenarios and the conditions that select between them, not pretending to know the future. Let me give you three scenarios — they are a synthesis of the kind of futures the chapter and the broader literature sketch, and the right column gives you the hinge question for each.
First, reform and renewal: the open order survives, but only by doing the thing it failed to do the first time — actually sharing the gains. That means serious compensation for the losers of globalization, robust safety nets, effective retraining and adjustment assistance, regional investment in the places that were hollowed out. The hinge question is brutal and honest: can domestic politics deliver compensation now, when it conspicuously failed to deliver it for forty years? Second, managed globalization: not a return to the hyper-globalization of the 1990s, but a slower, more guarded version — selective integration, friend-shoring among trusted partners, security carve-outs for strategic sectors, while trade and investment continue at a reduced, more deliberate pace. The hinge here is whether states can keep the security exceptions narrow, because every sector can be called strategic if you squint, and exceptions have a way of swallowing the rule. Third, fragmentation: the darkest scenario, in which the world economy splits into rival blocs along geopolitical lines, decoupling accelerates, and we forfeit large chunks of the efficiency gains that integration delivered. The hinge is whether great-power rivalry, especially between the United States and China, can be contained before security concerns simply override the logic of mutual gain.
The unifying point, in the callout, is the one I most want you to carry out of this course: the open economy is not guaranteed and it is not natural. It is a political achievement that can be sustained or squandered by political choices. And the single most important of those choices is the distributional one — whether the societies that host the system can share its gains widely enough to keep the coalition that supports it intact. That is why the distributional challenge in Section 2 was not just one challenge among several; it is, arguably, the master variable that determines which of these three futures we get. Now let me pull the analytical apparatus of the whole course together, because that apparatus is what lets you reason about questions like this one.

title: Achievements and Challenges of Global Capitalism
section: The Central Frame: Society-Centered vs. State-Centered
text:
The Central Frame: Society-Centered vs. State-Centered


Society-centered

The unit of analysis is domestic groups with competing economic interests
Policy is the outcome of who wins the domestic fight — firms, sectors, factors, voters
Explains distribution: who gains and loses, and who therefore lobbies and votes which way


State-centered

The unit of analysis is the state pursuing national goals — power, security, autonomy, development
Policy serves the national interest as the state defines it, sometimes against domestic groups
Explains strategy: industrial policy, security carve-outs, weaponized interdependence





This is the central analytic frame of the whole course. Almost every chapter handed you a society-centered and a state-centered lens. The skill is knowing which one a situation calls for — and seeing how they interact.




This is the capstone slide, and it is the single most important thing to fix in your mind before tomorrow’s final, because it is the organizing structure of the entire course. If someone stopped you in the hallway and asked what the analytical core of INTL 503 was, this is the answer: the recurring contrast between a society-centered approach and a state-centered approach to international political economy. We did not introduce these as two isolated theories in one week and then move on. We came back to this contrast in unit after unit, because it is the master distinction of the field.
The society-centered approach takes domestic groups as the fundamental unit. It says: to explain a country’s foreign economic policy, look inside the country at the competing economic interests — firms, industries, factors of production, classes, voters — figure out who gains and who loses from a given policy, and the policy you observe is the outcome of the political contest among them. Trade protection happens because import-competing groups out-organize free-trade groups; monetary policy reflects whoever wins the domestic fight between, say, exporters who want a weak currency and consumers who want a strong one. The society-centered lens is fundamentally about distribution and domestic politics. The state-centered approach takes the state itself as the fundamental unit, a purposive actor pursuing national goals — power, security, autonomy, long-run development — in a competitive international system. It says policy can serve the national interest as the state’s leaders define it, sometimes overriding what any domestic group wants. Industrial policy to build strategic capabilities, investment screening to block a rival’s access, sanctions and weaponized interdependence, central-bank arrangements designed for geopolitical leverage — these make sense through the state-centered lens, not the society-centered one.
The skill this course was trying to build, in the callout, is not memorizing which approach is “right” — neither is, in general. It is diagnostic. Given a real situation, which lens illuminates it, and how do the two interact? The most interesting cases, and the ones the final will reward, are where they collide: where a state’s strategic objective runs against a powerful domestic coalition, or where domestic distributional politics constrains what the state can do strategically. The backlash we discussed today is exactly such a collision — domestic distributional grievance, a society-centered phenomenon, driving a turn toward state-centered economic nationalism. If you can fluently switch between these two lenses and see where they meet, you have the core competency of this course. The next slide shows you how it threads through every unit.

Study move: for any chapter, ask “what’s the society-centered story, and what’s the state-centered story?” If you can fill both cells, you understand the unit.




This table is your study map for the cumulative final, so let me walk it row by row, because it shows you that the frame from the previous slide is not an abstraction I am imposing after the fact — it is genuinely how each unit of the course was built. Read each row as a pair: the society-centered story and the state-centered story for the same body of material.
Trade, Chapters 2 through 7: the society-centered story is Chapter 4 — who wins and loses from openness, and how that drives the demand for protection. The state-centered story is Chapter 5 — strategic trade and industrial policy, where the state intervenes to build national economic power regardless of any particular group’s preferences. Multinationals and FDI, Chapters 8 and 9: the society-centered story is firms lobbying and host countries bargaining over the terms of investment; the state-centered story is Chapter 9 and investment screening, where security concerns lead states to control or block foreign capital. The monetary system, Chapters 10 through 13: the society-centered story is Chapter 12, the domestic fight between exporters who want a cheap currency and consumers and importers who want a strong one; the state-centered story is Chapter 13 — credible commitment, central-bank independence, the trilemma as a constraint on state choice, and the dollar as an instrument of power. Development finance, Chapters 14 and 15: the society-centered story is how domestic coalitions shape borrowing and crisis response; the state-centered story is the IMF, conditionality, and how great-power influence shapes who gets rescued and on what terms. And the final unit — yesterday’s coercion class and today’s Chapter 16: the society-centered story is the distributional losers demanding protection; the state-centered story is weaponized interdependence and the broad subordination of efficiency to security.
Here is the concrete study move, in the callout, and I mean this literally for tomorrow. For any chapter on the exam, ask yourself two questions: what is the society-centered story here, and what is the state-centered story? If you can fill in both cells of the row, you understand the unit well enough for the applied section of the final. If you can only fill one, that is where to go review tonight. The applied policy question in particular will reward exactly this move — taking a contemporary scenario and analyzing it through both lenses, then staking out a defensible reading of how they interact. That is the skill. This table is the skill, laid out across the whole course. Now let me close, and tell you exactly how the final is built.

Let me close with the practical business of the final, because you deserve to start tomorrow knowing exactly what you are facing. Logistics first. title: Achievements and Challenges of Global Capitalism
text:
Closing the Course



Today’s Big Question — Global capitalism has delivered historic gains — can the system that produced them survive the backlash against them?





Key Empirical Take-aways


The achievements of globalization are real: a historic fall in poverty, convergence between nations
But the gains were unevenly shared, the growth path strains the planet, and the coalition behind openness is fracturing
The order’s future is a political choice, not destiny



A New Analytic Lense


The society- vs. state-centered frame — a lens for any IPE question, long after this class
Comfort moving between distribution (who wins/loses) and strategy (power and security)
The habit of asking, of any policy: whose interests, through which institutions, with what trade-offs?





Thank you for a breakneck but rewarding four weeks. See you online tomorrow at 8:10.





Let me gather the whole course around the Big Question one last time. Global capitalism has delivered historic gains — can the system that produced them survive the backlash against them? Here is where we landed, and I want to give you the honest, two-sided answer rather than a slogan in either direction. The achievements are real and enormous, and we should never let the current pessimism erase them: more than a billion people lifted out of extreme poverty, a historic convergence in incomes between nations, the rise of emerging Asia through integration rather than withdrawal. That is the most important material improvement in human welfare in history, and it happened under the open economic order. But the same system distributed its gains unevenly, imposing concentrated and persistent losses on workers and regions inside the wealthy democracies; the growth path that produced the gains strains the planet through a climate problem that is, at bottom, a collective-action problem we are structurally bad at solving; and the political coalition that sustained the order is fracturing under the weight of that distributional grievance and a turn toward security over efficiency. So the answer to the Big Question is genuinely open. The order’s survival is not a forecast we can read off the data. It is a political choice — above all, the choice of whether its gains can be shared widely enough to keep its supporting coalition intact.
And here is what I hope you carry out of this course, beyond any particular fact you will need tomorrow. The deepest thing this course gave you is the central analytic frame: the society-centered versus state-centered lens, and the fluency to move between them. That is a tool you will be able to point at any question in international political economy for the rest of your life — every trade war, every currency dispute, every sanctions regime, every investment-screening fight that shows up in the news. You now know to ask, of any economic policy: whose interests does it serve, through which institutions does it operate, and what trade-offs does it impose? That habit of mind — distribution and strategy, who wins and what’s at stake — is the real deliverable of these four weeks, and it outlasts the exam by a lifetime.
I will say plainly, with no hedging: this has been a genuinely good four weeks, and I have enjoyed teaching this group. Go work through the study guide, re-do those quizzes, re-read your writing, and get some sleep tonight. I will see you online tomorrow morning at eight-ten for the final. Good luck — you are ready.

title: Debt, Capital Flows, and Crisis in the Developing World
text:
Today’s Plan



Today’s Big Question


Foreign capital is supposed to finance development — so why does it so often end in crisis, and who decides who pays when it does?








Section
What we'll cover




1 · The Development Financing Problem
Why poor countries borrow abroad, and why lending to sovereigns is hard


2 · Institutions as the Answer
The World Bank and the IMF: lending where private markets won't


3 · Crises, Bailouts, and Conditionality
Latin America 1982 and Asia 1997 — who is rescued, on what terms


4 · Imbalances, Adjustment, and Power
Reserve hoards, Bretton Woods II, and who adjusts today


5 · Synthesis and Looking Ahead
The three themes together, the student presentation, and a bridge to coercion








A quick orientation, because today’s format is unusual. This is a combined session: Chapters 14 and 15 together. Oatley wrote them as a pair — developing countries and international finance, parts one and two — and rather than marching through them chapter by chapter, we are going to organize the day around three themes that run across both. Theme one: the IMF and the World Bank exist to help developing countries grow by solving a commitment problem that would otherwise keep investment capital away from the places that need it most. Theme two: when booms end in crisis, bailouts follow, and bailouts create a distributive fight over who is rescued and on what terms — that is where conditionality lives, and where the Latin American crisis of the 1980s and the Asian crisis of 1997 come in as evidence. Theme three: the crises left behind durable global imbalances, and those imbalances raise the question we ended on last Tuesday — when accounts must eventually balance, who bears the cost of adjustment?
Hold the Big Question the whole way through. Foreign capital should be developmentally good: it lets a poor country invest more than it can save. And yet the history of developing-country finance is a history of crises. Why? And when the crisis comes, who decides whether creditors take losses or citizens absorb austerity? Notice that second half of the question is political, and it is the half the three themes keep answering in different ways.
It is Monday, so we open with the usual in-class writing prompt and there is no quiz today — the last quiz was Friday, and the next assessment is the final. The reading pairing for today is the Ballard-Rosa, Mosley, and Wellhausen article, which one of you is presenting at the end of class, and the Planet Money episode about a hedge fund, a country, and a sailboat. Both will surface repeatedly before we get there.

title: Debt, Capital Flows, and Crisis in the Developing World
section: Before We Start: A Ten-Minute Write
text:
Before We Start: A Ten-Minute Write



Writing prompt. You advise the finance minister of a lower-middle-income country. Global interest rates are low, and foreign lenders are eager to extend credit on easy terms. The minister wants to borrow heavily to build ports, power, and rail.
Do you recommend borrowing? Name three things you would want to know before deciding. And if the loans go bad in five years, who do you expect will bear the cost — the lenders, the government, or the country’s citizens?






Write for about ten minutes from intuition and from the reading. We will return to your answers when we discuss conditionality — and again in the closing discussion.




Before any lecturing, take out a sheet and write for about ten minutes. The scenario: you are advising a finance minister in a lower-middle-income country. World interest rates are low, lenders are enthusiastic, and the minister sees a chance to finance a generation of infrastructure with foreign money. Three tasks. First, make a recommendation: borrow or hold back. Second, and this is where I want most of your effort, name the three things you would want to know before deciding. Push yourself past the obvious. The interest rate matters, yes — but think about what the money will be spent on, whether those projects will earn the foreign exchange needed to service foreign-currency debt, what happens if world interest rates rise, and how long the lenders’ enthusiasm is likely to last. Third, the question that will follow us all day: if it goes wrong, who pays? Foreign banks? The government? Taxpayers and wage earners who never signed the loan documents?
The reason I open here is that this is precisely the decision Mexican, Brazilian, and Argentine officials faced in the mid-1970s, and Thai and Korean officials in the early 1990s. In hindsight we know how those episodes ended. But the decision did not look reckless at the time — the money was cheap, the projects looked productive, and refusing foreign capital has real costs too, measured in schools not built and growth foregone. I want you to feel that the choice is hard before we study the wreckage. Keep what you write; we will pressure-test it against the chapters in the conditionality section, and I will ask a few of you to share.

title: Debt, Capital Flows, and Crisis in the Developing World
text:
The Savings Gap


Rising incomes require investment — and investment must be financed out of savings.

Poor countries save little: least-developed countries saved about 13.4% of national income (1970–2006), against 21.7% in high-income OECD countries
Low income → low savings → low investment → low income: a trap
Foreign capital lets a country invest more than it saves at home — each dollar of inflow adds roughly a dollar of investment (Bosworth & Collins 1999)




The record. Private capital never arrives in a steady stream. Markets swing between excessive caution and exuberance — flooding a country one year, shutting it out the next.












Figure 1







Start with why a developing country exposes itself to foreign capital at all, because the rest of the day is about the costs, and the benefit has to be clear first. Development requires investment — factories, ports, power grids, schools — and investment has to be financed out of savings. Poor countries, almost by definition, generate little saving: when incomes are low, most income goes to consumption. Oatley reports the comparison from the World Development Indicators: over 1970 to 2006, the least-developed countries saved about thirteen percent of national income, against nearly twenty-two percent in the high-income OECD. That gap is a trap. Low income means low savings, low savings mean low investment, low investment keeps income low. Foreign capital is the escape hatch: if savings can be imported, a country can invest more than it saves domestically and move to a higher growth trajectory.
The chart puts the underlying association in front of the students: each dot is a developing economy, plotting its average savings rate against its average growth rate over 1990 to 2019. The pattern runs upward. China, Korea, Malaysia, Thailand, and Indonesia — the high savers — are also the fast growers; Kenya, Senegal, and Pakistan, saving around ten percent of GDP, grew far more slowly; Mexico, Brazil, Argentina, and South Africa sit in the middle on both dimensions. Walk the logic: if savings finance investment and investment drives growth, this is what you would expect to see — and it is why the savings gap motivates borrowing abroad. Be honest about the limits: this is an association, not a law. Ghana grew respectably on very low measured savings; Korea’s savings are partly a consequence of its growth as well as a cause. The correlation does not settle causation. What matters for today is that a finance minister looking at this picture will conclude that scarce domestic savings are a binding constraint — and that foreign capital offers a way to relax it.
And the promise is quantitatively real. Bosworth and Collins found that a dollar of capital inflow produces roughly a dollar of additional investment — foreign capital adds to the savings pool rather than displacing it — and both IMF and World Bank studies from the early 2000s found that countries participating in international financial markets grew faster on average. Rodrik and others add an important caution: foreign capital does not guarantee higher growth. What it provides is the opportunity.
Then the bottom callout, which is the day’s whole problem in two sentences. Private capital never flows to developing countries in a steady stream. Markets swing between excessive concern about risk and excessive enthusiasm, so a country is flooded with capital one year and shut out the next. When you hear the case histories later, keep asking: was the problem that these countries used foreign capital, or the rhythm with which it arrived and left? Oatley’s answer, and mine, is that the rhythm is at least half the story — and that rhythm is set largely outside the borrowing country.

title: Debt, Capital Flows, and Crisis in the Developing World
text:
Four Channels of Foreign Capital



Foreign aid — official development assistance: grants and concessional loans from donor governments and multilateral agencies. In 2020: $114B bilateral + $47B multilateral
Commercial bank lending — syndicated loans at market (often floating) rates; the dominant channel in the 1970s
FDI and portfolio investment — ownership of productive assets vs. tradable stocks and bonds; two-thirds to three-quarters of all postwar flows were private
Remittances — money migrants send home to their families: nearly $702B in 2021, about four times all DAC foreign aid combined





Composition matters as much as volume. FDI is hard to withdraw; bank loans and portfolio flows can leave in an afternoon.






Remittances bypass the state entirely — household to household, and far less volatile than private capital flows.











Figure 2







Foreign capital comes through four channels, and the differences among them do real analytical work today. First, foreign aid — the formal term is official development assistance — grants and below-market loans from donor governments and from multilateral agencies. The 2020 numbers: about a hundred fourteen billion dollars in bilateral aid from the advanced countries plus forty-seven billion through multilaterals. The United States is the largest donor in absolute terms at roughly thirty-five billion, but among the least generous relative to income — about two-tenths of one percent of national income, compared with three to six times that share for the smaller northern European donors. Keep that pattern in mind for the institutions section, because aid has never been a purely charitable enterprise.
Second, commercial bank lending — syndicated loans, frequently at floating rates, which matters enormously later. This was the channel that dominated the 1970s. Third, foreign direct investment and portfolio investment. You know FDI from Chapters 8 and 9: a firm builds or buys productive assets it controls, which makes it hard to withdraw quickly. Portfolio investment is financial claims — stocks and bonds — which can be sold in an afternoon. Across the postwar period, private flows of these kinds have made up two-thirds to three-quarters of all capital reaching the developing world; aid is the smaller share, contrary to most students’ intuitions.
Fourth, remittances, which students consistently underrate. Nearly seven hundred two billion dollars in 2021 — roughly four times all DAC foreign aid combined. India received eighty-three billion, China fifty-nine, with the Philippines, Mexico, Egypt, and Pakistan close behind. Two features make remittances distinctive. They flow household to household, bypassing governments and firms — which means they bypass most of the political economy in this lecture. And they are far less volatile than private capital flows. So notice the callout on composition: because these channels behave so differently under stress, two countries taking in identical totals can face completely different crisis risks. That point is the hinge between this section and everything that follows.
The chart puts thirty years of these channels in one picture, for the developing world as a whole. Three observations to draw out. First, scale: total flows grew from under a hundred fifty billion dollars in 1990 to roughly one point eight trillion in 2021. Second, composition: FDI and remittances are the two big layers from the 2000s onward, and official aid — the green sliver — is the smallest of the four, confirming the point that most capital reaching the developing world is private. Third, behavior: watch the gold layer, portfolio flows. It swings hard year to year and actually turns negative in 2008, when investors pulled equity out of emerging markets during the global crisis — a preview of the volatility argument in section three. One honest caveat for the curious: commercial bank lending, the channel that dominates the 1970s story we tell next, is missing from this chart because no comparable aggregate series exists for the full period; the four channels shown are the ones the World Bank measures consistently, and the aid series currently ends in 2021.

title: Debt, Capital Flows, and Crisis in the Developing World
text:
Petrodollars and the Borrowing Boom


How the 1970s made bank lending the main channel of sovereign borrowing:

1973 oil shock: Saudi Arabia’s surplus jumped from $2.5B to $23B in one year
Exporters deposited the earnings — petrodollars — in Western banks
Banks lent the deposits to developing-country governments: petrodollar recycling
Oil importers borrowed rather than compress imports (~$260B in added costs over the decade)




Debt-service capacity — the ability to meet principal and interest payments out of export earnings — deteriorated: loans financed projects that earned no foreign exchange. By 1978, debt service took 38% of Latin America’s export revenue.












Figure 3








Developing-world foreign debt rose from $72.7B in 1970 to $586.7B in 1980 (Oatley, Table 14.3). The seven largest Latin American borrowers saw their debt increase tenfold by 1982.





Now the mechanism that turned commercial bank lending into the dominant channel and set up the first great crisis. It begins with oil. When OPEC quadrupled prices in 1973, the exporters earned surpluses far beyond what they could spend at home — Saudi Arabia’s current-account surplus jumped from two and a half billion dollars in 1973 to twenty-three billion in 1974, and averaged around fourteen billion for the next three years. Those earnings, deposited in Western commercial banks, are the petrodollars — a key term. The banks then had to do something with an enormous pool of deposits, and they lent it on to developing-country governments. That intermediation — oil earnings deposited in London and New York, then re-lent to Mexico City, Brasília, and Buenos Aires — is petrodollar recycling, also a key term.
The demand side mattered just as much. The same oil shock that enriched the exporters hit oil-importing developing countries hard — about two hundred sixty billion dollars in extra import costs over the decade, by Cline’s estimate. Governments committed to import-substituting industrialization would not compress imports and could not quickly raise exports, so they borrowed to cover the gap. And ISI itself generated appetite for capital: Latin American governments accounted for a third to half of total capital formation, ran state enterprises, and subsidized credit; by decade’s end the region’s budget deficits averaged nearly seven percent of GDP. The result is in the callout: developing-world debt went from about seventy-three billion dollars in 1970 to nearly five hundred eighty-seven billion in 1980, and the seven biggest Latin American borrowers saw a tenfold increase by 1982.
The chart shows the buildup region by region, in World Bank debt data. Two things to point out. First, the crimson layer: Latin America and the Caribbean took on far more of the new debt than any other region — its stock roughly septupled between 1970 and 1980 and kept climbing right up to the dashed line in August 1982, when Mexico told the U.S. Treasury it could not pay. Second, the debt did not stop growing after 1982 — the stack keeps rising through 1990 — because rescheduling stretched payments without forgiving principal, and arrears compounded; that is the lost-decade arithmetic we will see shortly. Note for precision: the current World Bank series totals somewhat less than the figures Oatley reports from an older data vintage — about sixty-four billion in 1970 versus his seventy-three, and about four hundred fifty versus his five hundred eighty-seven in 1980 — because country coverage and definitions have been revised; the shape of the boom is identical.
For a while it worked — Latin America grew five and a half percent a year through the late seventies. But watch the third key term: debt-service capacity, the ability to make principal and interest payments, conventionally measured against export earnings. It deteriorated steadily, because so much borrowed money went into projects that earned no foreign exchange — hydroelectric megaprojects serving domestic markets, military purchases, consumer subsidies. By 1978, debt service was already consuming thirty-eight percent of Latin America’s export revenue. The debt was payable only so long as new lending kept arriving. Hold that thought.

title: Debt, Capital Flows, and Crisis in the Developing World
section: The Obstacle: Lending to a Sovereign
text:
The Obstacle: Lending to a Sovereign


Sovereign lending is contracting without a court:

A government that borrows has an incentive not to repay once it holds the money
Lenders have no bankruptcy court and no sheriff — no way to compel a sovereign to honor the contract
So the borrower faces a commitment problem: it cannot credibly promise repayment, and it has incentives to overstate its ability to pay
Anticipating this, lenders lend less, at higher rates, or never





The hold-up problem. If lenders expect to be stiffed, the developmentally useful capital never flows — everyone is worse off. Political risk of this kind is a principal reason sub-Saharan Africa attracts so little private capital.






Same credible-commitment logic as central banks in Chapter 13 — now on the borrower’s side of the table.



🎧 Today’s podcast — Planet Money ep. 689, “A Hedge Fund, A Country, and A Big Sailboat.” A creditor tries to enforce a sovereign contract — by seizing a navy tall ship in Ghana.


Before the institutions make sense, you need the obstacle they exist to solve. Sovereign lending is contracting without a court. Walk the chain. A government that borrows has an incentive, once the money is in hand, to stop paying — repayment is costly and the funds are already spent. In ordinary lending, that temptation is held in check by law: a creditor can sue, seize collateral, force bankruptcy. Against a sovereign state there is no bankruptcy court and no sheriff. So the borrower faces a commitment problem — it cannot credibly promise to repay, because everyone understands the temptation it will face later — and it also holds private information, with every incentive to look more creditworthy than it is. Lenders anticipate all of this, and they respond by lending less, demanding higher rates, or staying away entirely.
That is the hold-up problem, and notice what it costs. The deal both sides want — capital flows in, projects get built, loans get repaid, everyone gains — fails to happen because the borrower cannot bind itself. The chapters make the development stakes concrete: default risk and political risk are a principal reason sub-Saharan Africa attracts so little private capital. The tragedy is capital that never arrives. This is the same credible-commitment logic we used for central banks on Friday, relocated to the borrower’s side of the table.
Now, today’s podcast belongs exactly here, because it shows what enforcement looks like when a creditor refuses to accept that there is no court. After Argentina’s default, the hedge fund NML Capital spent a decade pursuing repayment through litigation, and in 2012 persuaded a court in Ghana to detain the ARA Libertad, an Argentine navy training ship, when it docked there. A three-masted tall ship, held in an African port, as a debt-collection device. I assigned the episode because it makes the abstraction vivid: when your counterparty is a sovereign, seizing a sailboat is close to the outer limit of what a private lender can do. Keep the episode in mind — the holdout creditors will return when we discuss who bears crisis costs, because they are the distributive conflict in miniature.

title: Debt, Capital Flows, and Crisis in the Developing World
text:
The World Bank Family


Public institutions lend where private markets won’t — to borrowers markets would not touch:

The International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD), 1944: close-to-commercial rates, productive projects
The International Development Association (IDA), 1960: the concessional window for countries that cannot borrow on IBRD terms
Together they anchor the World Bank, the center of multilateral development finance
Regional development banks — Inter-American, African, Asian — extended the model region by region










Figure 4








Always Geostrategic The U.S. backed the IDA to preempt a rival UN agency; Kennedy’s Alliance for Progress used aid against Communism. In 2016 China launched the AIIB — and the U.S. declined to join.





Theme one begins here: both of today’s institutions exist to help developing countries grow by working around the hold-up problem — by supplying capital that private markets, for the reasons we just covered, will not supply. Start with the development-finance side. The International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, founded at Bretton Woods in 1944, lends at close-to-commercial rates to finance productive projects; in its first decade it mostly financed European reconstruction. The World Bank, as we use the term now, is the IBRD together with its affiliates. The problem, visible by the late 1950s, was that decolonization produced dozens of new states that could not borrow on private markets and would not qualify under the Bank’s normal terms either. The institutional answer was the International Development Association, created in 1960 — the concessional window, offering long maturities and near-zero interest to the poorest members. Alongside it came the regional development banks — the Inter-American, African, and Asian Development Banks — replicating the model closer to the borrowers. Multilateral aid quadrupled between 1956 and 1970, and bilateral aid more than doubled.
Use the diagram to fix the institutional map before the names start flying. The container on the left is the World Bank Group; the two boxes inside it — the IBRD and the IDA — are what people mean when they say “the World Bank”: one balance sheet lending at near-commercial rates, one lending on concessional terms, same building. The navy box beside it is the IMF, created at the same 1944 conference; students constantly conflate the two, so draw the line now — the Bank finances development projects, the Fund lends to governments in balance-of-payments crises, and the Fund is the institution the rest of today runs through. The bottom row shows the same model replicated region by region: the Inter-American, African, and Asian Development Banks during the Cold War decades, the EBRD after 1991 for the post-communist transition (the EBRD is my addition for completeness; Oatley does not discuss it), and, in gold, the AIIB — the China-led bank from 2016 that the callout picks up.
But keep the second callout in view, because the aid regime was never purely a technical fix. The United States championed a concessional window inside the World Bank in part to preempt a proposed UN agency where developing countries would have held more influence. Kennedy’s Alliance for Progress directed aid to Latin America explicitly to forestall Cuban-style revolutions. Aid was a Cold War instrument as much as a development instrument, and where it flowed tracked donor interests. That doubleness — institutions that solve a real market failure and serve their principal shareholders’ politics — is going to follow us all day, and it has a sharp contemporary edition: in 2016 China launched the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank. The United States declined to join and urged its European allies to stay out; most joined anyway. Oatley describes the episode as one more sign of economic power shifting toward Asia.
