Strong states centralize authority, coordinate across agencies, and offer few access points to lobbyists. Japan is the textbook strong state — MITI, now METI, working with the Ministry of Finance, used “administrative guidance” to move capital from steel and shipbuilding in the early postwar years into high-technology in the 1970s, and many credit this for the Japanese miracle. France is the other strong-state case, with its insulated bureaucracy and its “National Champions” strategy — though notice Oatley’s honest detail that the French national computer champion, Machines Bull, failed to become competitive, an early reminder that strength guarantees coherence, not success. The United States is the canonical weak state: federalism, separated powers, and porous agencies create so many channels for lobbying that officials struggle to act coherently in any “national interest.” And yet — this is the move I want students to catch — the U.S. runs a large de facto industrial policy through the back door of national defense: Pentagon R&D and procurement underwrote computing, the internet, and, as we’ll see in a moment, the early semiconductor industry. That defense loophole is the historical seed of today’s “economic security” turn. Last point, and it’s the double edge: insulation is exactly what lets a strong state plan long-term and, crucially, withdraw protection once an industry matures — but it’s also what removes the feedback that would tell the state it has chosen badly. Strength is not the same as good judgment.

title: A State-Centered Approach to Trade Politics
section: When Markets Have Room for Only a Few
text:
When Markets Have Room for Only a Few
Strategic-trade theory (Krugman; Brander & Spencer 1985) extends the infant-industry logic to oligopoly — industries with room for only a handful of firms.



Big scale + steep learning ⇒ only 2–3 firms worldwide can survive (aircraft: ~2; autos: ~8)
These firms earn rents — profits above what the same capital and labor earn elsewhere
Whoever hosts the firm captures the rents as national income
So there’s a zero-sum race: only a few countries can win





Absent intervention, the first mover wins — early scale and experience let it deter every later entrant, even one that would have been just as good.







The core policy idea: a government can use a subsidy to shift the rents from a foreign firm to a domestic one — making its own country richer at the rival’s expense.




Strategic-trade theory is the intellectual high-water mark of the case for intervention, and it’s associated above all with Paul Krugman and with the 1985 Brander–Spencer model. It takes the infant-industry insight and drops it into a world of oligopoly. The setup: when economies of scale and experience are severe enough, the world market only has room for a handful of firms — two for long-haul commercial aircraft, about eight for autos. Because entry is so limited, these firms earn rents: returns above what the same labor and capital would earn in their next-best use. The nationalist implication is this: whichever country hosts the firm captures those rents as higher national income, in the form of better-paid workers and higher returns to investors. Since only a few firms can exist, only a few countries can capture the rents, which sets up a zero-sum competition among states over who gets the industry. Who wins, absent any government action? The first mover. By entering early and racing down the scale-and-experience curve, the incumbent builds a cost advantage that deters later entrants — even an entrant who, given the same head start, would have been every bit as competitive. That’s a crucial and somewhat unfair feature: the winner wins because it was first, not because it was better. And that opens the radical policy door. If a government can subsidize a domestic late-entrant enough to make entry credible, it can alter which firm survives — shifting the rents, and the national income, from the foreign incumbent to the home firm. This is rent-shifting, and it follows a genuinely beggar-thy-neighbor logic: one country’s gain is the other’s loss. Consider it as a game.

title: A State-Centered Approach to Trade Politics
text:
The Rent-Shifting Game








Figure 3








A subsidy of 25 relocates rents of 125 and induces the rival’s exit. This is the formal case that intervention can raise national income.




This is Krugman’s 1987 illustration, Oatley’s Figure 5.1, and it’s worth building live on the board if you have time. Two firms, one American and one European; the market supports only one producer. Each chooses “produce” or “don’t.” Look at the left matrix first. If only one produces, it earns 100 and the other earns 0 — those are the two equilibria, the top-right cell where the U.S. produces and Europe stays out, and the bottom-left where Europe produces and the U.S. stays out. If both produce, they split a market too small for two and both lose money, here minus 5 each. So the outcome is indeterminate in theory and settled in practice by who moves first: the incumbent produces, the entrant rationally stays out because entering only earns it a loss, and the incumbent keeps the 100. Now the right matrix. Suppose the European government commits a subsidy of 25 to its firm whenever it produces. Re-read Europe’s payoffs: if the U.S. produces, Europe now earns 20 instead of losing 5 by producing; if the U.S. stays out, Europe earns 125. Producing is now better for Europe no matter what the U.S. does — it’s a dominant strategy. The American firm, anticipating this, knows Europe will produce, so its best response is to exit. The single equilibrium flips: Europe captures the market and earns 125. Tally it for the European treasury: it spent 25 in subsidy to relocate 100 of rents — plus the extra 25 — onto its own soil. A small public outlay levers a large private rent away from the rival. That is the formal heart of strategic-trade theory, and one can see why it unsettled free-trade economists: here is a model in which a subsidy does not merely protect a domestic industry but displaces the foreign one. Now I want you holding two questions, because we’ll spend the back half of the lecture on them. First, does this actually work outside the diagram? Second — and notice the payoff structure already hints at it — what happens when the other government subsidizes as well? The result depends on the rival government remaining passive.

title: A State-Centered Approach to Trade Politics
section: Rent-Shifting in the Wild: Chips and Jets
text:
Rent-Shifting in the Wild: Chips and Jets








Figure 4








The U.S. built both industries first — through defense procurement. Japan (MITI) and Europe (Airbus) then used protection and subsidy to capture a share of the rents. This generates international political conflict over industrial policy. Previously, the US used the GATT/WTO largely to try to reverse other countries’ industrial policies. Now, US is increasingly taking a “if you can’t beat ’em, join ’em” attitude.




Strategic-trade theory isn’t only a diagram; Oatley gives two cases where the rent-shifting story fits the record reasonably well. Semiconductors first. The U.S. got there first, and notice how — not through a deliberate industrial policy but through defense. Pentagon purchases absorbed up to 100 percent of early semiconductor output and still 40 percent into the late 1960s, which let American firms race down the learning curve; by the early 1970s they held something like 98 percent of their home market and most of Europe’s. Then, from the 1970s, Japan’s MITI targeted semiconductors with exactly the strategic-trade toolkit: tariffs and quotas to keep American chips out, restrictions on foreign investment so U.S. firms couldn’t jump the barrier, procurement favoring Japanese chips, and R&D subsidies across dozens of projects. The result is the left panel — American firms held only about 20 percent of the Japanese market, and by 1986 Japan had captured roughly 46 percent of global semiconductor revenue while the U.S. share fell to about 40. The rents moved. The right panel is the aircraft mirror image. Boeing and McDonnell Douglas dominated postwar, again partly on the back of military contracts — the 707 was derived from a military tanker. Then in 1967 France, Germany, and Britain launched Airbus and poured in somewhere between 10 and 18 billion dollars, about 75 percent of development cost. Airbus went from zero to roughly 30 percent of the large-aircraft market by 1990, outsold Boeing for the first time in 1994, and reached rough parity by the mid-2000s. A large slice of the industry’s rents transferred from the U.S. to Europe. Two honest caveats for students. First, these are the cases that fit; the failures — Machines Bull, Concorde, many MITI initiatives — are less often cited, and selecting on successes is exactly the trap we’ll name in the objections section. Second, look at what actually founded both industries: not visionary economic planning but defense spending. The state was already in these industries for security reasons before anyone articulated a competitiveness rationale — which is precisely the issue the modern debate reopens.

title: A State-Centered Approach to Trade Politics
text:
Same Tools, New Objective








Figure 5








For two centuries the case for industrial policy was economic — growth, productivity, competitiveness, rents. Since roughly 2017 the dominant case has become strategic — supply-chain resilience, chokepoints, and not depending on a rival.




Here is the pivot the whole lecture has been building toward, and it’s the one I most want you to leave with. The toolkit of industrial policy — subsidies, procurement, protection, state credit — has barely changed in two hundred years. What has changed, and changed sharply in the last decade, is the justification. From Hamilton through postwar Japan through 1980s strategic-trade theory, the argument was fundamentally economic: build the industry because it raises growth, productivity, competitiveness, captures rents, employs people in high-wage jobs. The yardstick was national income. Read the Sullivan and policy language of the 2020s and the yardstick has moved. The CHIPS Act, the Inflation Reduction Act’s clean-energy provisions, the October 2022 export controls — these are defended primarily as security measures: keep critical supply chains resilient, deny a rival access to advanced technology, and don’t let the country be dependent on an adversary for things it cannot live without. The timeline color shift on the slide is the argument in one image — crimson competitiveness on the left bleeding into navy security on the right. Two cautions so we don’t caricature this. The shift is in emphasis, not kind; competitiveness arguments never vanished, and security arguments are old — recall that the U.S. semiconductor and aircraft industries were founded on defense money. And the dating is rough; you can put the inflection at the 2017 National Security Strategy, or the 2018 tariffs, or COVID’s supply-chain shock, or the 2022 invasion of Ukraine. The point is not a precise date but a reframing: the same policy that an economist would judge by whether it raises national income is now judged by whether it keeps the nation safe. Those are different tests, they do not always agree, and much of today’s discussion depends on distinguishing them.

title: A State-Centered Approach to Trade Politics
section: Why Policy Makers Now See Dependence as Vulnerability
text:
Why Policy Makers Now See Dependence as Vulnerability
Trade always created security externalities — but whether interdependence contributes to peace or vulnerability depends on the geopolitical environment.


Liberal Internationalism (1990s)
Interdependence as mutual restraint. Gains from trade bind rivals together. Depending on others is efficient.
Economic Security (now)
Networks have chokepoints. The state that controls a hub — the dollar, SWIFT, advanced chips — can deny a rival access or surveil the flows passing through it (Farrell & Newman 2019, weaponized interdependence).




Trade follows the flag. Free trade is more likely within alliances than across them — because trade with an ally strengthens you, trade with a rival strengthens them (Gowa & Mansfield 1993; Hirschman 1945).



The same dependence — on foreign chips, e.g. — may be interpreted as efficient specialization among allies and as a strategic liability among rivals.


If the rationale has shifted from competitiveness to security, the obvious question is: why now? Why does relying on foreign suppliers, which the gains-from-trade logic of Chapter 3 celebrates as efficient specialization, suddenly look like a threat? The IPE answer is that trade has always carried security externalities — consequences for the balance of power, not just for income — and how heavily those weigh depends on the geopolitical environment. Bring in two literatures. First, Gowa and Mansfield’s 1993 work, building on Albert Hirschman back in 1945: trade isn’t politically neutral, because the gains from trade are also gains in national capability. Trade with an ally strengthens a partner whose strength helps you; trade with a rival strengthens an adversary whose strength threatens you. So free trade clusters within alliances — “trade follows the flag” — and states worry about relative gains, about who is strengthened more, especially across a rivalry. Second, Farrell and Newman’s 2019 concept of weaponized interdependence, which updates Hirschman for the network age. Modern economic networks — dollar clearing, the SWIFT messaging system, the chip supply chain — aren’t flat; they run through a few central hubs. Whoever controls a hub gets two powers: the chokepoint, the ability to deny a rival access, and the panopticon, the ability to see everything flowing through. Put the two ideas together and you get the modern anxiety in one line, the bottom of the slide: the very same dependence reads completely differently depending on who’s at the other end. Relying on Taiwanese or Dutch chips among allies looks like sensible specialization; relying on a strategic rival for the same input looks like granting them control of a chokepoint. Nothing about the economics changed — what changed is the assessment of intent and the structure of the network. That is why the security environment, not the trade theory, is the decisive factor in today’s policy.

title: A State-Centered Approach to Trade Politics
section: The New Toolkit — and the New Vocabulary
text:
The New Toolkit — and the New Vocabulary





Instrument
What it does — and why




CHIPS & Science Act (2022)
USD 52.7B for domestic semiconductors (USD 39B in subsidies, a 25% tax credit, plus R&D), with "guardrails" barring expansion in China.


Inflation Reduction Act (2022)
Hundreds of billions in clean-energy subsidies with domestic-content rules — climate policy *and* competition with China rolled together.


Export controls (Oct. 2022 →)
Bars sales of advanced chips and chip-making tools to China. The goal is not to capture rents but to deny a rival a capability.


"Small yard, high fence"
Sullivan's framing (2023): restrictions stay narrow and security-focused; a "New Washington Consensus" replaces reflexive liberalization.










Note the shift in objective. Classic industrial policy seeks to build domestic winners; export controls seek to deny rivals a capability.




This is the concrete contemporary toolkit, and it’s worth being precise because the article our presenter covers lives inside it. The CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 put 52.7 billion dollars behind domestic semiconductor manufacturing — about 39 billion in direct subsidies, a 25 percent investment tax credit, and roughly 13 billion for R&D and workforce — with “guardrails” that bar recipients from expanding advanced manufacturing in China. The Inflation Reduction Act layered on hundreds of billions in clean-energy subsidies with domestic-content requirements, which is fascinating precisely because it fuses three rationales at once — climate, jobs, and competition with China — and different advocates sell it with whichever rationale suits them. Then, two months after CHIPS, the October 2022 export controls, which are a genuinely different instrument: they do not try to build an American chip champion, but to deny China access to advanced chips and the tools to make them. Jake Sullivan’s 2023 Brookings speech gave this whole posture its slogans — “small yard, high fence,” meaning the restrictions are supposed to be narrow and security-focused rather than a general blockade, and a “New Washington Consensus” to replace the reflexive free-trade consensus of the 1990s. I want students to catch the shift in objective at the bottom of the slide, because it is analytically important. Classic industrial policy is constructive — it tries to build winners, and you can at least argue it against a market-failure benchmark. Export controls are destructive — they try to deny a rival a capability — and that has almost no market-failure justification at all; it’s straightforwardly an exercise of power. When we get to the objections, keep asking which kind of policy we’re evaluating, because the build-a-winner kind and the deny-a-rival kind fail in different ways and for different reasons.

title: A State-Centered Approach to Trade Politics
text:
Can the Line Be Drawn?








Figure 6








The slippery-slope risk: once “security” considerations overriding the market, almost any industry can invoke it. A criterion that applies to everything constrains nothing — and protectionist interests have strong incentives to adopt the language of security.




This slide is the Big Question made operational, and it’s the one I’d most like to spend discussion time on. Lay industries along a spectrum. At the left, things that are genuinely just economic — consumer solar panels, where the case is competitiveness or climate, not survival. At the right, things almost everyone agrees are security — munitions, the rare-earth magnets that go into guided weapons, nuclear and weapons technology — where you would not want to depend on an adversary at any price. The analytical action is all in the shaded middle: EV batteries, critical minerals, advanced semiconductors. Chips are the perfect hard case because they are simultaneously a consumer good, the foundation of economic competitiveness, and a military necessity — the same fab makes the chip in your phone and the chip in a missile. So is a chip subsidy industrial policy or defense policy? The honest answer is that you often cannot cleanly separate them, and that ambiguity is not a footnote — it’s the central governance problem. Here is the slippery-slope concern, and it is why economists are wary. The market-failure discipline established earlier — name the distortion, use the narrowest tool — has real constraining force. “National security” has almost no bite as a limiting principle, because with enough imagination every industry can tell a security story: food security, energy security, even “freedom” of various supply chains. If everything can be labeled security, then security stops doing any analytical work, and the label becomes exactly what a protectionist lobby reaches for when the economic argument has failed. Recall the Chapter 4 logic: concentrated producers are superb at organizing. Provide such interests with a rationale that suspends ordinary cost-benefit scrutiny, and the risk becomes evident. And note the irony I flagged earlier: Korea’s heavy-and-chemical drive, the cleanest success story in the new evidence, was itself launched for security reasons — North Korean provocations and a U.S. troop drawdown — and it happened to also build competitiveness. So security and competitiveness rationales aren’t always rivals; sometimes they point the same way. The analytical skill we are building is distinguishing the case where they genuinely align from the case where “security” functions as a pretext.

title: A State-Centered Approach to Trade Politics
section: Three Reasons Industrial Policy Often Fails
text:
Three Reasons Industrial Policy Often Fails



Picking winners (the knowledge problem). Effective intervention requires identifying the right sector and calibrating the right subsidy. Governments are frequently poor at both, and misjudged targeting misallocates capital.
Rent-seeking & capture (Krueger; Olson). Once subsidies are available, firms have incentives to compete for them through lobbying rather than innovation; political connections, not productivity, can determine who benefits.
The exit problem. Protection meant to be temporary tends to persist, as protected firms become a standing constituency for its continuation.





The underlying difficulty: industrial policy is designed for an idealized government but implemented by the actual one — subject to capture, short time horizons, and difficulty reversing failed commitments.







Dani Rodrik (most pro-industrial policy elite economist): the decisive question is less whether a state can pick winners than whether it can let losers go.




Now the case for the prosecution, because a good IPE student should be able to argue both sides fully. Three classic objections. First, the knowledge problem, popularly “picking winners.” Even granting that intervention can work in theory, the government has to do two hard things: identify which sector actually offers the long-run gains, and calculate the right size of subsidy. Get the sector wrong or the dose wrong and scarce capital is committed to an unviable sector — and the track record includes Concorde and Machines Bull. Second, and politically deeper, rent-seeking and capture, the logic of Anne Krueger and Mancur Olson. The moment subsidies are available, you change what firms optimize for: effort shifts from making a better product to lobbying for a larger subsidy, and the firms that win are the ones best at politics, not the ones best at production. Industrial policy can quietly convert an economy’s most capable firms into its most effective lobbyists. Third, the commitment problem — the “temporary” protection that never sunsets. The entire welfare case rested on removing the tariff once the infant grew up, but a protected industry becomes a concentrated, organized constituency for its own continued protection, and democratic governments rarely have the political will to withdraw it. Taken together, these yield the claim in the callout, which I regard as the single most important sentence in the objections: industrial policy is usually designed for an idealized government — far-sighted, disinterested, technically brilliant — and then implemented by the actual government we have, which is lobby-captured, electorally myopic, and structurally reluctant to acknowledge a failed commitment. Rodrik’s reframing is the constructive version and worth giving students: stop asking whether the state can pick winners, which demands near-omniscience, and ask the more achievable thing — can it let losers go? A system with hard budget constraints and real exit can tolerate many poor choices; a system that cannot terminate its failures will accumulate losses regardless of how well it selects. That’s also a usable evaluation rubric for the CHIPS-era programs: not “did they choose chips correctly” but “is there any mechanism to stop if it isn’t working?”

title: A State-Centered Approach to Trade Politics
text:
The Theory Suggests Targeted Interventions
The strategic-trade case for subsidies is not only hard to implement but theoretically limited.





Change one assumption…
…and the optimal policy reverses





Firms compete on QUANTITY (Cournot)
Brander & Spencer (1985): SUBSIDIZE your firm
Subsidy shifts rents home


Firms compete on PRICE (Bertrand)
Eaton & Grossman (1986): TAX your firm
Subsidy is counterproductive; the opposite policy is optimal










If an assumption as subtle as quantity- versus price-competition reverses whether the optimal policy is a subsidy or a tax, a government cannot easily know which case it faces. Accounting for rival retaliation and general-equilibrium effects weakens the result further.
If you are going to “do” industrial policy, probably should only procede where market failures are biggest and where strategic benefit of internalizing capabilities highest.




The objections so far are about implementation, but there’s a deeper problem: the theory that licenses the subsidy is itself brittle, and this is the critique that made even Krugman cautious about his own creation. Brander and Spencer’s 1985 result — subsidize your national champion to shift rents home — depends on a specific assumption about how the firms compete, namely Cournot competition, where firms choose quantities. Eaton and Grossman showed in 1986 that if you instead assume Bertrand competition, where firms choose prices, the optimal policy reverses: now you should tax your own exporter, not subsidize it. Consider how damaging this is. The very same model, the same firms, the same rents — and flipping one assumption that is essentially invisible to a policymaker flips the recommendation from “subsidize” to “tax,” from help to hurt. Brander and Spencer offered an example, not a general law. And the fragility compounds: in general equilibrium, subsidizing the strategic sector pulls resources out of other industries, taxing them implicitly; and the whole result assumes the rival government sits still, when in reality it retaliates with its own subsidy and both treasuries simply transfer money to the same oligopolists, and the rents are dissipated. So the honest verdict on strategic-trade theory is the one Oatley reaches: it does not give robust, usable support for the claim that intervention reliably raises national income. It tells you intervention could help under precise conditions you usually can’t verify, with tools whose correct sign you can’t determine, against a rival that does not remain passive. It functions less as a policy prescription than as a caution.

title: A State-Centered Approach to Trade Politics
section: Does Industrial Policy Work? Recent Evidence
text:
Does Industrial Policy Work? Recent Evidence
Recent causal studies (Juhász, Lane & Rodrik 2024) reach more favorable conclusions than the earlier, largely skeptical literature — though their findings are strongly conditional.


Evidence it can work

South Korea’s HCI drive (1973–79): Lane shows it durably shifted comparative advantage into heavy industry — benefits spread downstream and persisted after the policy ended.
Juhász (Napoleonic blockade), Hanlon, and others find real, lasting effects in well-identified cases.


…but read the fine print

These are successes studied carefully, not a promise of replication.
Korea’s HCI was security-driven (North Korea, U.S. troop drawdown) — and still cost-laden and contested.
Evidence of success in one case does not establish transferability; context, state capacity, and exit discipline are decisive.





The position emerging from this literature is conditional rather than categorical: industrial policy can succeed under conditions that must be specified. The debate has moved from whether it works to when and how.




I don’t want to leave students with a caricature in either direction, because the actual research frontier is more interesting than “industrial policy good” or “industrial policy bad.” For decades the empirical literature was mostly skeptical, leaning on correlational studies and cautionary tales. The recent wave — Juhász, Lane, and Rodrik survey it in their 2024 Annual Review piece, “The New Economics of Industrial Policy” — uses modern causal-inference tools and reaches a more positive, though carefully hedged, conclusion. The flagship case is Nathan Lane’s study of South Korea’s Heavy and Chemical Industry drive from 1973 to 1979. Using the input-output structure of the economy, Lane shows the policy genuinely shifted Korea’s comparative advantage into targeted heavy industries, that the gains propagated to downstream users of those intermediates, and — the striking part — that the benefits persisted even after the program ended. Juhász’s work on the Napoleonic blockade as a natural experiment in protection, and several other well-identified studies, point the same way: in specific cases, well-designed promotion left a lasting mark. But teach the fine print as carefully as the headline. First, these are successes examined closely; they do not certify that the next program will work — there is an obvious selection issue in which episodes receive careful econometric treatment. Second, look again at Korea: the HCI drive was launched for national-security reasons, after North Korean provocations and a U.S. troop drawdown, which is a notable illustration that the security and competitiveness rationales we tried to separate were fused in the very case that most strongly supports industrial policy. And it was still enormously costly and remains contested. So the mature position, the one I want you to be able to defend, is neither the free-marketeer’s “never” nor the planner’s “always.” It’s “sometimes, under conditions you have to specify” — state capacity to choose and to exit, a real market failure or security rationale, and discipline to stop. The field has moved from arguing about whether industrial policy works to arguing about when and how — which is exactly the question contemporary semiconductor policy is now testing.

title: A State-Centered Approach to Trade Politics
text:
Oatley’s Verdict: A Fatal Flaw?



No microfoundations. The model asserts states act for national welfare. But why would autonomous officials enrich society rather than themselves? (Think Versailles.) What’s the reward structure?
Autonomy is overstated. Even Japan’s MITI served the LDP’s big-business base. “Autonomous” states still answer to some coalition.
Strategic-trade theory is weak. As shown above: sensitive to assumptions, hard to target, and reversible in sign.





Oatley’s view: the missing microfoundations are a fatal flaw. The approach tells us autonomous states will act — but not how they’ll act, or why toward welfare.






The fix may be to combine approaches: states with real autonomy, but acting within limits set by the coalition that keeps them in power.





Before the handoff, Oatley’s own balance sheet, because he is notably hard on the approach he’s just taught. Three weaknesses. First and most fundamental, the lack of microfoundations. The state-centered approach asserts that autonomous states act to raise national welfare, but it never explains why they would. An autonomous ruler — picture Versailles — has at least as much incentive to enrich himself and his circle as to enrich society. So what reward structure makes individual officials choose national welfare? It can’t be elections, because that collapses you back into the society-centered model. It might be security competition — states that build strong economies survive — but nobody has worked out how that systemic pressure translates into the specific resource-allocation choices of particular bureaucrats. Oatley considers this gap serious enough to call it a fatal flaw: the approach can tell us an autonomous state will act, but not how it will act or why toward welfare rather than self-dealing. Second, the autonomy assumption is overstated in the other direction. Even Japan, the strongest of strong states, had a MITI whose industrial policy conspicuously favored big business — which happened to be the LDP’s political base. Was that the national interest, or the ruling coalition’s interest presented as the national interest? Even insulated states answer to someone. Third, the theoretical engine, strategic-trade theory, is weak in the ways we just dissected. Oatley’s constructive suggestion, and it’s the right note to end the analysis on, is synthesis: don’t choose between Chapters 4 and 5, combine them. Expect states to have genuine autonomy and objectives of their own, but exercised within boundaries set by the societal coalition that keeps them in power. That hybrid — autonomous within limits — is closer to how trade politics actually works than either pure model, and it’s the lens I’d carry into the article.

title: A State-Centered Approach to Trade Politics
section: Next: Semiconductors as the Test Case
text:
Next: Semiconductors as the Test Case



We have developed the theory of state-centered trade. The presentation now applies it to the central industrial-policy case of the present moment — semiconductors.





Questions to hold during the presentation

Is CHIPS-era policy best read as competitiveness, security, or both — and can Bown & Wang tell them apart?
Where on today’s spectrum do chips fall — and who decides?
Does the case look more like Korea’s HCI success or like a picking-winners / rent-seeking trap?
What would count as this policy working — and is there an exit?


Student-led article presentation
Bown, C. P. & Wang, D. (2024). “Semiconductors and Modern Industrial Policy.” Journal of Economic Perspectives 38(4): 81–110.
Then
In-class writing prompt


This is the handoff, and it’s deliberately a clean one — I’ve given you the scaffolding, and I’ve stayed off the article itself so our presenter has the floor and the case material to work with. Everything today was the theory of state-centered trade; Bown and Wang take that theory to the single most important industrial-policy episode of our moment, semiconductors, which is why I paired it here. Don’t summarize the chapter back at the presenter — instead carry these four questions in, because they’re the lecture’s concepts turned into a worksheet for the article. One: when Bown and Wang describe the CHIPS Act and the export controls, are they best understood as competitiveness policy, security policy, or an inseparable fusion — and do the authors manage to draw the line we struggled to draw? Two: where do chips actually sit on our competitiveness-to-security spectrum, and who gets to make that call? Three: does the semiconductor push look more like Korea’s HCI drive — a security-motivated bet that durably built comparative advantage — or more like the picking-winners-and-rent-seeking trap the critics warn about? And four, the Rodrik test: what would it even mean for this policy to have worked, and is there any mechanism to stop if it hasn’t? After the presentation and discussion we’ll close with the in-class writing prompt, where you’ll stake out and defend a position of your own. Let me turn it over to our presenter.

title: A State-Centered Approach to Trade Politics
section: Writing Prompt: Competitiveness, Security, or Both?
text:
Writing Prompt: Competitiveness, Security, or Both?



Writing prompt. Bown and Wang just walked you through the CHIPS Act and the semiconductor export controls — the single largest industrial-policy bet of the last decade.
Stake out a position: is this competitiveness policy, security policy, or an inseparable fusion of the two — and does it matter which? Use today’s competitiveness-to-security spectrum and the Rodrik test (what would count as this policy working, and is there an exit) to defend your answer.






Write for about fifteen minutes, using at least one named concept from today (OLI, infant-industry logic, the competitiveness-to-security spectrum, or the Rodrik test). Then a brief share-out.




This is the payoff for the whole session — don’t let students retreat into just summarizing the chapter or the article. They need to take a side. The trap to watch for: many will want to say “it’s obviously security” because that’s the government’s stated rationale, without engaging the possibility that security framing is doing political work — suspending the usual scrutiny that would apply to ordinary industrial policy. Push anyone who lands there to name what evidence would change their mind. Conversely, students who say “it’s obviously just protectionism in security clothing” need to engage the genuine national-security logic — the chip supply chain really is concentrated in a handful of vulnerable, geopolitically exposed sites (Taiwan chief among them). The best answers will hold both possibilities in tension rather than resolving too quickly.

title: The Political Economy of International Trade Cooperation
text:
Today’s Plan



Today’s Big Question


Why is trade cooperation so hard even when everyone would gain — and what kind of institution does it take to make it possible?








Section
What we'll cover




1 · Why Trade Cooperation Is Hard
The puzzle Oatley opens with — does the world still need the WTO?


2 · The Economic Case for Trade
Gains from trade, comparative advantage, and why protection destroys welfare


3 · The Bargaining Problem
Spatial bargaining, linkage, costly signals, and outside options


4 · The Enforcement Problem
The prisoner's dilemma and why anarchy traps governments in protection


5 · The WTO as Incentive-Compatible Enforcement
How iteration and reciprocity solve the cooperation problem


6 · The DSM in Action: U.S.–Brazil Cotton
Brazil v. United States — how international rules work through domestic politics


7 · Student article presentation
Bown & Keynes 2020 on the Appellate Body crisis


8 · Writing prompt and discussion
Apply today's framework to a current case

title: The Political Economy of International Trade Cooperation
section: Does the World Still Need the WTO?
text:
Does the World Still Need the WTO?
For seventy years, the WTO and the GATT have anchored the international trade system. The institution is now under sustained pressure.


Signs of erosion:

The Doha Round has produced little since 2001
Members pursue trade goals through mega-regionals outside the WTO framework
Aggressive bilateralism has eroded multilateral rule-making


Most analysts argue the WTO is still needed. The argument rests on a theory of international cooperation that we develop today.




Cooperation is difficult even when all parties stand to gain, because anarchy makes agreements hard to enforce.




Open by naming the contemporary tension Oatley puts at the top of the chapter. Doha has produced almost nothing since 2001; the world’s largest economies have spent a decade pursuing mega-regionals (TPP, TTIP, RCEP, CPTPP) outside the WTO framework; and the Trump era added an explicitly bilateralist approach that walked away from multilateral disciplines. Yet the textbook claim — and most analysts agree — is that governments still need the WTO. Why? Because cooperation on trade is genuinely hard, and we don’t have a substitute institution. That’s what we’re going to develop today: the theoretical reason why an institution like the WTO has to exist if open trade is going to survive. Three steps: gains from trade, the cooperation problem, the WTO solution. Move briskly — we only have 5 minutes for this section. The point is to plant the puzzle, not solve it.

title: The Political Economy of International Trade Cooperation
text:
Comparative Advantage



Every country gains from trade by specializing in what it produces relatively well, even if it produces everything at higher cost than its trading partner.





What is not required

An absolute cost advantage in any good
The United States gains from trading with China even if U.S. firms could produce every good more cheaply


What is required

Different opportunity costs across the same goods
Each country specializes in the good for which it gives up less of others
Both countries consume beyond what autarky allowed



This is the Core Idea slide. State the principle plainly before any geometry. Most students have heard “comparative advantage” but very few can articulate it correctly. The distinguishing claim is that absolute advantage is not required — even a country that’s worse at producing everything still gains from trade, because what matters is the relative costs across goods within each country. Set this up clearly here and the rest of the section follows. If students leave today with one thing about trade theory, this is it.

title: The Political Economy of International Trade Cooperation
text:
The Production Possibility Frontier
The PPF shows everything a country could produce, given its labor and capital.
Its slope is the opportunity cost: how much of one good must be given up to make one more of the other.








Figure 1






Anchor the comparative advantage discussion in the PPF. Walk through the U.S. example from Oatley: if the U.S. throws everything at computers, it can make 100 million. If it throws everything at shirts, it can make 300 million. The line connecting those points is the PPF — every combination on the line is achievable. The slope is the opportunity cost: to make one more computer, the U.S. has to give up 3 shirts. We’re using constant opportunity costs (a straight line) to keep things simple; Oatley notes most contemporary models use diminishing returns (a curve), but the political-economy logic is the same either way. Don’t dwell on the geometry — students will see it again with China and then with both countries together. Just make sure they grasp that the line shows a trade-off, not a list of choices.

title: The Political Economy of International Trade Cooperation
text:
China Has a Different Frontier
Same logic, different opportunity costs — because China has different factor endowments (more labor, less capital).








Figure 2






China’s PPF is much steeper. China can make 400 million shirts if it specializes, but only 20 million computers — a function of its factor endowments (abundant labor, less capital). The opportunity cost of a computer in China is 20 shirts, compared to 3 in the U.S. Note: I am using Oatley’s numbers exactly — these are illustrative, not empirical. The pedagogical point is that the two countries have different opportunity costs, not the specific numbers. Different opportunity costs are what make trade beneficial. If both countries had identical PPFs, there would be no gains from trade — no specialization possible. The geometry of comparative advantage hinges on the gap between the two slopes (3 vs. 20). That gap is where the gains come from.

title: The Political Economy of International Trade Cooperation
section: Trade Lets Both Consume Beyond Autarky
text:
Trade Lets Both Consume Beyond Autarky
The two countries agree on a trade price (Oatley uses 6 shirts per computer).
Each fully specializes. Both consume on a higher indifference curve than autarky allowed.








Figure 3






Reproduces Oatley’s Figure 3.3 in spirit — full specialization with trade. Walk through the numbers: U.S. specializes in computers (produces 100 million), exports most of them, gets shirts in return. China specializes in shirts (produces 400 million), exports most, gets computers in return. At the trade price of 6 shirts per computer, U.S. consumption moves from (60 computers, 120 shirts) under autarky to roughly (75, 150) with trade. China’s consumption moves from (13, 140) to (25, 250). Both countries are unambiguously better off — they consume more of both goods than they could produce on their own. That’s the welfare engine that makes the rest of the chapter (and the rest of the field) make sense. If trade weren’t mutually beneficial, the cooperation problem wouldn’t matter. Because it is, the cooperation problem becomes a puzzle worth solving — which is what the WTO does.

title: The Political Economy of International Trade Cooperation
section: Where Does Comparative Advantage Come From?
text:
Where Does Comparative Advantage Come From?





Ricardian model (Ricardo, 1817)


Comparative advantage comes from differences in labor productivity — i.e., technology.
Countries specialize where their technology gives them an edge.
Key insight: technology, not endowments, drives the pattern.







Heckscher-Ohlin (H-O) model (early 20th c.)


Comparative advantage comes from factor endowments — the relative supply of capital, labor, land.

Capital-abundant countries → capital-intensive goods (autos, aircraft)
Labor-abundant countries → labor-intensive goods (apparel)

Key insight: who owns the abundant factor wins from trade.












Figure 4






Two workhorse models. Ricardo (early 19th c.) said comparative advantage comes from technology — Britain has better looms, so Britain makes cloth more productively than Portugal even if both have the same labor. Heckscher-Ohlin (early 20th c.) said it comes from factor endowments — Britain has more capital, so Britain specializes in capital-intensive goods, while Portugal with more labor specializes in labor-intensive goods. The bar chart below illustrates the H-O intuition with Oatley’s example: in auto manufacturing, labor is only about 25–30% of costs, with capital dominating; in apparel, labor takes the lion’s share. The H-O punchline is the one that matters most for political economy: the owners of the abundant factor gain from trade, while the owners of the scarce factor lose. In the U.S., that means capital-abundant industries (and capital owners) gain from trade; labor-abundant ones (and lower-skilled workers) lose. Hold onto that thought — it’s exactly the kind of distributional asymmetry that drives the politics in Chapter 4. We don’t need to do the full Stolper-Samuelson theorem today, but the intuition is: trade isn’t neutral within a country, even when it’s net-positive overall.

title: The Political Economy of International Trade Cooperation
text:
Trade Policy and Welfare
Standard introductory microeconomics, not in Oatley. The left panel shows the welfare consequences of opening a closed economy to trade; the right panel shows how a tariff partially reverses them.








Figure 5








Opening to trade transfers area A from producers to consumers and creates area B as new welfare. A tariff partially reverses this: area A is transferred back to producers as new producer surplus, area C is collected by the government, and areas B and D are destroyed as deadweight loss.




This slide isn’t in Oatley but it’s the strongest economic argument for trade. Set up the small open economy: world price is below domestic autarky price; the country imports the difference. A tariff raises the domestic price above the world price. Producers respond by producing more (Q1 → Q2). Consumers respond by buying less (Q4 → Q3). Imports shrink. Government collects tariff revenue on what’s still imported (rectangle C). Now the welfare accounting: producers gain area A (their surplus increases because they get a higher price). Government collects area C (tariff revenue). But consumers lose A + B + C + D (their surplus falls by a much larger trapezoid). Net welfare change: gains are A + C; losses are A + B + C + D; net is −B − D. Areas B and D are pure deadweight loss — production we didn’t need at this cost, and consumption that doesn’t happen because the price is artificially high. This is the punchline: protection doesn’t transfer welfare from consumers to producers. It transfers some welfare to producers and government, AND destroys some welfare entirely. That’s why “free trade is good” isn’t just an ideological claim — it’s a welfare arithmetic claim. If we go back to the cooperation problem from earlier, this is what’s at stake: when governments fail to cooperate, they leave B and D on the table. The cost of WTO failure isn’t abstract; it’s measurable in lost welfare.

title: The Political Economy of International Trade Cooperation
text:
What This Theory Assumes
The standard comparative-advantage argument rests on three contested assumptions:





Market clearing


Prices and wages adjust freely; labor markets clear; no persistent unemployment.
Trade adjustment costs in practice can persist for decades and remain geographically concentrated.







Constant or decreasing returns


Markets are competitive rather than oligopolistic.
Trade in aircraft, semiconductors, and software is dominated by a small number of firms operating under increasing returns to scale.







Neutral terms of trade


Relative prices do not systematically favor some producers over others.
The Prebisch-Singer hypothesis argues that commodity exporters face deteriorating terms of trade against manufactured-goods exporters.







We will return to each of these assumptions when we cover development models and trade strategy.




This is a signposting slide — flagging that the theory we just walked through makes assumptions that aren’t always true. Three big ones. (1) Market clearing: standard trade theory assumes prices and wages adjust to keep labor employed. In reality, the China Shock literature (Autor-Dorn-Hanson and others) shows that trade adjustment can be slow and geographically concentrated, with displaced workers not finding equivalent employment for years or decades. (2) Constant or decreasing returns to scale: the textbook story assumes competitive markets — many firms, no one with market power. Modern trade in aircraft, semiconductors, pharmaceuticals, software is dominated by a small number of firms with massive economies of scale. That’s “new trade theory” (Krugman and others) — strategic interaction, market power, government intervention can shape who wins. Different politics, different policy implications. (3) Neutral terms of trade: the model assumes the relative prices of traded goods don’t systematically favor some producers. Prebisch and Singer argued in the 1950s that commodity exporters (developing countries) face deteriorating terms of trade against manufactured-goods exporters — a key intellectual foundation of import-substitution strategies in Latin America and elsewhere. We don’t have time to do these critiques justice today. Just flag them so students aren’t shocked when they show up later. We’ll revisit when we cover development.

title: The Political Economy of International Trade Cooperation
text:
Distribution Within Countries



Distributional conflict over trade is both interstate and intrastate. Country-level accounts of “winners” and “losers” obscure the within-country coalitions that produce national trade positions.





Between countries
Some countries gain more from a given agreement than others. Bargaining power determines the distribution (Section 3).

Within countries
Industries, regions, and factor owners gain and lose unevenly.
U.S. agriculture is heavily protected and subsidized despite farmers comprising roughly 1.5% of the population. The bicameral Senate gives Wyoming the same representation as California, amplifying the political power of rural producers.




Intrastate distribution is the subject of next lecture (Chapter 4). For today: “the U.S. position” in any negotiation is the position of the domestic coalition with sufficient political voice to define it.




This slide is critical and worth slowing down for. The standard trade-theory presentation talks about country-level gains and losses, which makes it sound like the political problem is just “U.S. vs. China” or “developed vs. developing.” But that’s only half of it. The other half — and arguably the more important half for politics — is within-country distribution. Even when comparative advantage says the U.S. gains overall, those gains go to some American workers, firms, and regions while other American workers, firms, and regions lose. The political question isn’t just “do we gain on net?” — it’s “which Americans gain, and which lose, and which group has more political power?” Big Ag is the canonical U.S. example. Farmers are tiny — about 1.5% of the population. But agriculture is one of the most heavily protected and most heavily subsidized sectors in the U.S. economy. Why? Because the bicameral system in the U.S. Senate gives each state two senators regardless of population, and farm-state senators wield enormous power over farm-state legislation. Wyoming (population 580,000) gets the same Senate representation as California (population 39 million). That structural feature of American political institutions massively amplifies the political power of rural producer interests. We’re going to spend a lot of time on this in Chapter 4 — society-centered theories of trade politics, Stolper-Samuelson, coalitions, the Ricardo-Viner / specific-factors model. For today, just plant the flag: when we say “the U.S. position” in trade negotiations, we don’t mean some abstract national interest. We mean whichever domestic coalition has the political voice to define the U.S. position. That’s a much messier story than the textbook lets on.

title: The Political Economy of International Trade Cooperation
section: Why Governments Do Not Liberalize Unilaterally
text:
Why Governments Do Not Liberalize Unilaterally



Trade gains exist in principle, but governments rarely cut tariffs without reciprocal concessions. The next slide develops a spatial model of why.





The unilateral problem

Domestic producer coalitions lose from open markets
Unilateral liberalization gives up domestic protection without securing foreign market access for exporters
The government moves away from its political ideal point


The bargained alternative

Governments exchange market-access commitments
A spatial model (next slide) maps the trade-offs in two dimensions
Today we focus on bargaining power and the conditions under which impasses are resolved



Quick recap since we did the bargaining geometry in detail Day 2. The key intuition: if a government just unilaterally drops its tariffs, it gives up the domestic political support of protected producers without getting anything in return for its exporters. So unilateral liberalization moves the government away from its political ideal — which is why governments don’t do it. Liberalization happens through trade agreements where both sides commit. The 1934 Reciprocal Trade Agreements Act in the U.S. is a great example of this logic at work — Congress delegated tariff-cutting authority to the President precisely because reciprocal cuts mobilized exporter constituencies that would otherwise stay silent. We don’t need to do that history again today; just remember the principle. Now we move to two new pieces of analytical equipment: linkage (how impasses get broken), and the signaling vocabulary (cheap talk vs. costly signals).

title: The Political Economy of International Trade Cooperation
text:
The Bargaining Space
Each axis is the level of tariff protection one side controls. Bargaining outcomes are points in this space.








Figure 6








Each circle is an indifference curve around one side’s ideal point, drawn with radius equal to the distance from that ideal point to the status quo. Points inside the circle are preferred to the status quo by that side. Where the two circles overlap, both sides prefer the outcome to the status quo — the joint-gains lens.




Build the diagram with the students. Two-dimensional issue space: horizontal axis is the level of tariff protection on U.S./EU agriculture, vertical axis is the level of tariff protection on G-20 manufactures. Higher in either direction means more protected. The status quo at Doha was high tariffs in both, so it sits in the upper-right. Each side has an ideal point in the opposite quadrant: the U.S./EU want to keep agricultural protection (high X) while opening up G-20 manufactures (low Y), so the U.S./EU ideal sits in the lower-right. The G-20 wants the mirror: low U.S./EU agricultural protection (low X) and high protection on its own manufactures (high Y), so the G-20 ideal sits in the upper-left. Now draw a circle around each ideal point with radius equal to the distance from that ideal point to the status quo. Any point inside that circle is preferred to the status quo by that side, because it is closer to their ideal point. The intersection of the two circles — the lens — is the set of outcomes both sides prefer to the status quo. That’s where bargaining can produce an agreement. Three minutes here; this is the analytical setup for what comes next. Linkage enlarges the bargaining space by adding issues, expanding the dimensions in which a lens can be found. Costly signals communicate which point in the lens each side will actually accept. Outside options change the location of acceptable deals by changing what “no deal” is worth to each side.

title: The Political Economy of International Trade Cooperation
text:
Linkage



Linkage bundles unrelated issues into a single negotiation. It is the principal mechanism by which large multilateral trade rounds reach agreement.





Why single-issue bargaining stalls

Each side has a politically protected sector on which it will not concede
The two-dimensional bargaining space is too narrow to contain a Pareto improvement
Negotiations terminate at the status quo


Why bundled bargaining can succeed

Combining agriculture, manufactures, services, and intellectual property creates room for cross-issue trade-offs
A concession on agriculture can be offset by a gain on services
The Uruguay Round (1986–1994) is the canonical case and produced the WTO itself





The Uruguay Round, the GATS, and the TRIPS agreement exist because linkage allowed issues that could not pass standalone to be bundled with issues on which both sides preferred movement.




Linkage is one of the most important moves in international cooperation theory and it’s worth slowing down on. The intuition: imagine two countries that both refuse to budge on a single issue — say agriculture. They’re stuck. The bargaining space on that one dimension has no Pareto improvement that both sides will accept. But add a second issue, say services or intellectual property, and suddenly the bargaining space expands. One side might be willing to concede on agriculture if they get a big win on services. The Uruguay Round is the textbook case. The U.S. wanted developing countries to commit to intellectual property protection (TRIPS) and services market access (GATS). Developing countries wanted advanced economies to open their agriculture markets and clothing markets. Neither would happen standalone — but bundled together, they did. The WTO itself is a product of that bundling. Without linkage, none of this gets done. Two implications for thinking about contemporary trade politics. First: when negotiations stall on a single issue, you should expect the political path forward to involve bundling — adding issues to expand the space of possible deals. Second: linkage is also why trade agreements have gotten more controversial. Tying together agriculture and IP and labor standards and environmental rules creates richer deals — but also means that anyone with a grievance on any of the linked issues has a reason to oppose the whole package. The trade-policy backlash since the 2000s is partly about linkage.

title: The Political Economy of International Trade Cooperation
section: Bargaining as a game of Signaling
text:
Bargaining as a game of Signaling





Incentives to misrepresent


Each side has private information about its reservation price (what it would actually accept).
Revealing the truth weakens your position (other side will only offer your reservation price), so each side has every reason to misrepresent how flexible they are.







Cheap talk


Statements that cost nothing to make (“this is our final offer”) are not credible.
Because anyone could say them, they convey no information about your real position.







Costly signals


Actions that would not be taken by a bargainer with different private information.
Walking away from the table, building outside options, accepting short-term political pain — these are costly because they’re real, and that’s exactly what makes them credible.







The 2008 G-20 walkout at the Doha Round, discussed in Oatley, is the canonical illustration of a costly signal in trade bargaining.




This is the cleanest vocabulary slide of the lecture — get the three terms locked in. Start with the bargaining problem: each side has private information about its reservation price (the worst deal it would still accept). If you reveal that information, your bargaining partner just offers you the minimum. So each side has an incentive to misrepresent — to claim its reservation price is higher than it really is. The problem is that everyone knows everyone has this incentive. Which means simple verbal claims — “this is our final offer” — are cheap talk: they cost nothing to make, anyone could make them, and they convey no information. The way to actually transmit information about your real position is through costly signals — actions that you would not take if your real reservation price were lower than what you’re claiming. Walking out of negotiations is the classic example. Building outside options is another. Accepting domestic political pain to demonstrate commitment is a third. The 2008 G-20 walkout at Doha is the textbook case — and Oatley walks through it in detail in the “A Closer Look” box. I don’t need to re-explain it here; just mention it as the illustration. Students have read the chapter. The key conceptual point: bargaining theory predicts that what people say matters less than what they’re willing to do, because actions reveal information that words can’t.

title: The Political Economy of International Trade Cooperation
section: Bargaining Power: Patience and Outside Options
text:
Bargaining Power: Patience and Outside Options



The largest economy is not always the strongest bargainer. Bargaining power derives from the ability to credibly walk away from a deal, which depends on patience and outside options.





Patience

Both sides lose utility from delay, but not equally
A more patient government can hold out for outcomes closer to its ideal point
Patience comes from political stability, low domestic pressure, and longer time horizons


Outside options

After 2008, the U.S. and EU pursued TPP, TTIP, and EU-Pacific agreements
Each RTA raises the value of WTO failure and lowers the price a country will pay for a multilateral concession
The 2008 G-20 walkout would have worked only if the U.S. and EU lacked alternatives; the alternatives existed, and Doha did not finish





A bargainer with patience or with credible outside options can credibly walk, and therefore can credibly demand more.




This is the central logical link of Section 3 — bargaining power as the ability to credibly walk away, which depends on patience and outside options. Cover both. Patience: both sides lose utility from delay, but not equally. A government with a stable mandate, long time horizon, and low domestic pressure can hold out for more. A government facing an election in six months, a domestic political crisis, or a coalition partner threatening to bolt is impatient — and impatient negotiators settle for worse outcomes. Patience is partly structural (political institutions, election cycles) and partly strategic (you can sometimes manufacture patience by removing yourself from the table). Outside options: the parallel mechanism. If your next-best alternative to a deal is bad, you’ll accept worse terms. If your next-best alternative is good, you can hold out. In trade, the next-best alternative to a multilateral WTO deal is a regional or mega-regional — bilateral or plurilateral agreements that capture some of the gains without requiring 164-member consensus. Once the U.S. and EU started seriously pursuing mega-regionals after 2008 — TPP and TTIP were both major Obama-era initiatives — the value of a Doha deal to them dropped. Why pay big concessions to G-20 countries in Geneva when you can get most of what you want bilaterally with strategic partners? That’s a major reason Doha never finished. And when India and China walked out in 2008, the walkout didn’t work because the U.S./EU had alternatives. A walkout is only credible as a costly signal if the other side has no outside options. India and China misjudged the bargaining setting. The next slide adds a twist most textbooks don’t cover: smaller and developing countries can also use RTAs strategically.

title: The Political Economy of International Trade Cooperation
text:
RTAs as Developing-Country Leverage



Arvind Subramanian, in Trade Talks ep. 215 (Day 1 podcast), argues that RTAs are not only leverage for advanced economies. Developing countries can use them strategically against China.





The conventional view

Outside options favor whoever holds them
Advanced economies have historically held more of them


Subramanian’s argument

By signaling willingness to deepen ties with non-Chinese partners, developing economies transmit a costly signal to Beijing about market access
The mechanism is the same as in the previous slide; the direction of leverage is different





Bargaining power accrues to whichever side can credibly walk away, regardless of which side that is.




This is a really important addition to Oatley because the textbook tells the bargaining-power story in a one-directional way — advanced economies have outside options, developing countries don’t, end of story. That’s increasingly not true. Subramanian, in the Day 1 Trade Talks podcast episode (ep. 215, which students listened to as part of Day 1 prep), makes the case that RTAs are also a tool developing countries can use against recalcitrant trade partners — and specifically against China. The argument: China has been slow to liberalize market access for foreign firms in many sectors. Smaller and developing economies that want better China access have limited individual leverage. But if they collectively signal willingness to deepen trade ties with non-Chinese partners — through bilateral agreements, regional integration, supply-chain reorientation — that’s a costly signal to Beijing. It tells China: continue dragging your feet and we’ll route around you. Same theoretical mechanism we just talked about — outside options as bargaining leverage — but the power flow is different. This matters for thinking about contemporary trade politics. Indonesia, India, ASEAN states, even Latin American countries can use trade diversification strategically. They’re not just price-takers in a system designed by advanced economies. (Paraphrase rather than quote — and the link to the podcast is in the schedule. Don’t push more details than this; we don’t have time and the students have heard the episode.)

title: The Political Economy of International Trade Cooperation
section: Reaching an Agreement Is Not Enough
text:
Reaching an Agreement Is Not Enough



Once an agreement is reached, each side has a unilateral incentive to defect: to retain its own tariffs while the other side cuts theirs. The prospect of receiving the sucker payoff (liberalizing while one’s partner does not) deters governments from signing in the first place.





The structure

Both sides have agreed to liberalize
Either can renege after signing
The international system lacks a third-party enforcer
What sustains compliance?


The model
The prisoner’s dilemma formalizes the situation:

Mutual cooperation maximizes joint welfare
Each player prefers to defect when the other cooperates
Anticipating mutual defection, neither cooperates



This is the conceptual bridge from bargaining (Section 3) to the WTO solution (Section 5). Even if governments can find a deal both sides prefer to the status quo — and stretch the bargaining space with linkage, signal credibly with costly signals, etc. — they still face the enforcement problem. Once they sign the deal, each side has a unilateral incentive to cheat. To keep its own protected sectors closed while exploiting the other side’s market opening. The fear of being on the receiving end of that — the “sucker payoff,” where you opened up but they didn’t — is enough to prevent cooperation from happening in the first place. The textbook frames this as the international cooperation problem and uses the prisoner’s dilemma to formalize it. We’re going to walk through that game theory carefully in the next few slides — it’s worth taking the time because the cooperative escape (iterated PD with tit-for-tat) is the exact theoretical foundation of the WTO’s Dispute Settlement Mechanism.

title: The Political Economy of International Trade Cooperation
section: The Prisoner’s Dilemma Applied to Trade
text:
The Prisoner’s Dilemma Applied to Trade










Figure 7





G-20 preference order: (P, L) > (L, L) > (P, P) > (L, P). EU is symmetric.

Best response logic
G-20

If EU plays Liberalize → G-20 prefers Protect (yields P, L over L, L)
If EU plays Protect → G-20 prefers Protect (yields P, P over L, P)
Protect is therefore a dominant strategy

EU (by symmetry)

Protect is also dominant for the EU
Both rational players choose Protect
The game terminates at (P, P)





Both sides know they would be better off at (Liberalize, Liberalize). Individual rationality nonetheless drives them to (Protect, Protect). The equilibrium is collectively suboptimal.




This is the analytical core of the section. Walk through the matrix first, then the best-response logic, ending at the Nash equilibrium label on the (P, P) cell.
The matrix: G-20 is the row player, EU is the column player. Each has two strategies, Liberalize or Protect. Four cells: (L, L) mutual cooperation with joint gains; (L, P) G-20 opens its market but EU does not — G-20’s worst outcome, the sucker payoff; (P, L) G-20 keeps protection while EU opens — G-20’s best outcome, the temptation payoff; (P, P) mutual protection, the status quo. Preference order for G-20: (P, L) > (L, L) > (P, P) > (L, P). EU is symmetric.
Best response logic — walk through it methodically. If the EU plays Liberalize, G-20 compares (L, L) and (P, L) and prefers Protect because (P, L) is its best outcome. If the EU plays Protect, G-20 compares (L, P) and (P, P) and prefers Protect because (L, P) is its worst outcome. Protect is therefore a strict dominant strategy for G-20: optimal regardless of what the EU does. By symmetry, the same logic gives Protect as a dominant strategy for the EU. Both rational players choose Protect, and the equilibrium is (P, P).
Now name the equilibrium. (P, P) is a Nash equilibrium because neither player can unilaterally improve their payoff by deviating: unilateral deviation from (P, P) yields the sucker payoff for the deviator. The result is a stable but suboptimal outcome — both players prefer (L, L) but neither can move there alone. This is the formal expression of the cooperation problem and the setup for everything in Section 5: how iteration and reciprocity allow governments to escape this trap.

title: The Political Economy of International Trade Cooperation
section: Two Properties of the (P, P) Equilibrium
text:
Two Properties of the (P, P) Equilibrium





Pareto suboptimal


At least one player could be made better off without making anyone else worse off.

Both sides prefer (L, L) to (P, P)
(L, L) is reachable in principle
Yet they don’t reach it








Nash equilibrium


No player can unilaterally improve their payoff by changing strategy.

G-20 deviation from (P, P) yields (L, P), its worst outcome
EU deviation from (P, P) yields (P, L), its worst outcome
Neither player has a unilateral incentive to deviate








Together, these properties define the cooperation problem. The (Protect, Protect) outcome is stable (no unilateral incentive to deviate) yet collectively suboptimal (both sides prefer Liberalize, Liberalize). Individual rationality produces collective dysfunction.




Two formal definitions worth nailing down. Pareto suboptimal: an outcome from which at least one player could be made better off without making anyone else worse off. (P, P) is Pareto suboptimal because both players strictly prefer (L, L). There’s a Pareto improvement available, but the game doesn’t get there. Nash equilibrium: an outcome at which no player can unilaterally improve their payoff by changing strategy. (P, P) is a Nash equilibrium because if either player switched alone to liberalize, they’d get the sucker payoff. The deviation makes them worse off. So neither has any incentive to deviate. The kicker: these two properties together are what makes the cooperation problem hard. (P, P) is stable (Nash) AND bad (Pareto suboptimal). It’s stable because it’s bad — if it were Pareto optimal, no one would want to deviate; here, deviating unilaterally makes you worse off even though deviating jointly would make everyone better. This is the formal definition of what it means to be trapped. Conceptual point for students: when you see “X happens even though Y would be better for everyone,” the underlying analytical structure is almost always something like this — individually-rational behavior producing collectively-irrational outcomes. The PD is a workhorse model not just for trade, but for climate, security, public goods provision, antitrust, you name it.

title: The Political Economy of International Trade Cooperation
text:
Iteration



A one-shot Prisoner’s Dilemma traps countries in a suboptimal equilibrium (Protect, Protect). But states are long-lasting: they play repeatedly, and often with the same partners. In an iterated Prisoner’s Dilemma, cooperation can become rational under certain conditions.





One-shot game

Defection yields the temptation payoff once
No future round, no future punishment
Cooperation is irrational


Iterated game

Defection today invites punishment tomorrow
The stream of cooperation payoffs (L, L) can exceed a one-time defection gain
Cooperation is sustainable if players are sufficiently patient
This result is the Folk Theorem in game theory



Iteration changes everything. In a one-shot PD, defection is rational because there’s no future. You take the temptation payoff and move on. But in real life, the U.S. and EU don’t negotiate once — they negotiate over and over, year after year, decade after decade. Iteration introduces a future. If you defect today, your partner can punish tomorrow. That changes your payoff calculation. You’re no longer comparing one defection against one cooperation — you’re comparing a stream of future cooperation payoffs against a single defection payoff plus future punishment. If you discount the future at a reasonable rate and your partner uses a credible punishment strategy, cooperation becomes the rational choice. This is the analytical foundation of every cooperative institution we have. The Folk Theorem in game theory makes this formal: in an iterated PD with sufficiently patient players and credible punishment strategies, cooperation can be sustained as an equilibrium. Note: the result depends on patience (low enough discount rate) and a credible punishment strategy. We need to talk about both — and we’ll see in a moment that the WTO institutionally supplies (or at least supports) both conditions.

title: The Political Economy of International Trade Cooperation
text:
Three Conditions for Cooperation (Axelrod-Keohane-Oye)





1. Iteration


The same parties must play repeatedly and expect future interactions. Without iteration, no future round can discipline present behavior.







2. Reciprocity


Players need a strategy that rewards cooperation and punishes defection. The canonical example is Axelrod’s tit-for-tat.







3. Future-orientation


Players must value future payoffs enough that anticipated punishment disciplines current behavior. A sufficiently low discount rate sustains cooperation; a high one collapses the game back to one-shot.







Robert Axelrod (1984), The Evolution of Cooperation; Robert Keohane (1984), After Hegemony; Kenneth Oye (1986), Cooperation Under Anarchy.




Three conditions, each citing the foundational works in international cooperation theory. Iteration: the same parties have to play repeatedly. If you only deal with someone once, they have no reason to keep their word — and you have no way to punish them later. The future has to exist in some real sense for the game theory to work. Reciprocity: the cooperator needs a strategy that rewards cooperation and punishes defection in measurable ways. Tit-for-tat — play whatever your partner played last round — is the canonical example, and Axelrod’s computer tournaments in the early 1980s showed it consistently outperforms more complicated strategies. The key feature: nice, retaliatory, forgiving, and clear. Future-orientation: the players have to care about future payoffs. If they fully discount the future — if a payoff tomorrow is worth zero today — the iterated game collapses back to a one-shot game and cooperation fails. Bring the citations: Axelrod’s Evolution of Cooperation (1984) is the empirical and theoretical foundation. Keohane’s After Hegemony (1984) is the IR application. Oye’s edited volume Cooperation Under Anarchy (1986) brought together a generation of scholars working in this tradition. These are the texts that defined how IR thinks about cooperation for the next 40 years. The WTO is, in many ways, the institutional embodiment of this literature.

title: The Political Economy of International Trade Cooperation
section: How the WTO Supplies These Conditions
text:
How the WTO Supplies These Conditions


Iteration




Stable membership: 164 members and few exits in over seventy years
Repeated rounds: eight completed, the ninth (Doha) ongoing
Periodic policy reviews of every member by its peers




The same governments deal with each other repeatedly, year after year.

Reciprocity (information and standards)




MFN and national treatment supply bright-line standards against which behavior can be evaluated
Transparency requirements apply to trade remedies, safeguards, and non-tariff barriers
The WTO publishes systematic data on every member’s tariffs and NTBs




Tit-for-tat requires that each side observe when its partner has defected. The WTO supplies the information.




Future-orientation is a property of governments themselves, not something the WTO can supply. When governments stop valuing future trade cooperation, the iterative logic of the institution erodes. (More on this when the student presents Bown & Keynes 2020.)




This is the central conceptual argument of the lecture’s second half. The WTO doesn’t enforce trade agreements directly — it supplies the institutional conditions under which governments can enforce agreements among themselves. How? By providing iteration and information. Iteration: the WTO has had stable membership for decades. 164 countries belong; almost no one has ever left. So when the U.S. and Brazil negotiate today, they know they’ll be negotiating again next year and the year after. There’s a stream of future interactions to discipline current behavior. The WTO also runs regular bargaining rounds (eight completed, plus Doha ongoing) and conducts trade policy reviews for every member every few years. Every member’s behavior is under continual scrutiny. Reciprocity needs information. To play tit-for-tat, you have to know when your partner has cheated. The WTO provides this through several institutional features. MFN and National Treatment are bright-line rules — you can tell when someone violates them. Trade remedies, safeguards, and NTBs all have transparency requirements — countries have to notify the WTO when they impose them. And the WTO secretariat publishes systematic data on tariffs and trade barriers. This is the information infrastructure that makes credible reciprocity possible. What the WTO can NOT supply is the third condition: future-orientation. That’s a property of governments themselves.
